attempts.answer:
# Executive summary

There is persuasive SSA evidence that climate risk disclosure has been expanding and is associated with stronger governance and nonfinancial transparency, but direct causal estimates of improved financial reporting quality (FRQ) for Sub‑Saharan African non‑financial firms remain limited and uneven. <cite id="64f34a72-0">Across SSA, ESG/climate disclosure has grown in response to investor stakeholder demands and access-to-capital incentives, yet empirical confirmation of its impacts on reporting quality has been thin</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-1">A multi-country SSA sample shows substantial heterogeneity in environmental disclosure quality, with average Environmental Disclosure Index scores around a quarter of a full scale and only partial coverage of core risk indicators such as carbon emissions and regulatory compliance</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">In South Africa, JSE-mandated integrated reporting increased disclosure of human, social/relationship, natural, and intellectual capital and improved integrated reporting quality over time</cite>, <cite id="cea1a99e-2">with studies documenting greater disclosure breadth and positive associations between higher integrated reporting scores and better accounting performance</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-3">Carbon and climate-related disclosures have also been embedded into annual reporting requirements via King III/IV and JSE rules, with research motivated by the expectation that such disclosures affect financial outcomes through legitimacy channels</cite>. 

On effects and selection: <cite id="9ea234ab-2">A structured review of 134 empirical articles finds that climate disclosure quality and determinants are linked to financial implications, but also flags concerns about symbolic reporting and greenwashing</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">It documents rising convergence with TCFD and IFRS S2, yet emphasizes that effectiveness in reflecting underlying performance is mixed</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-4">Recent assessments of readiness for IFRS S1/S2 in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa highlight persistent gaps in consistency, comparability, and quality, with capacity and enforcement constraints as key barriers</cite>. Put together, the balance of evidence suggests that adoption of climate risk disclosure in SSA is associated with measurable improvements in reporting transparency and quality where enforced (e.g., South Africa), and that higher-quality reporters are more likely to adopt due to governance and legitimacy incentives; however, robust SSA‑specific causal estimates on financial accounting quality (e.g., accrual quality, restatements, audit report quality) are scarce, and symbolic or greenwashing risks can mute or reverse benefits if capacity and assurance mechanisms are weak. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">Where disclosure is high‑quality and decision‑useful, studies report positive financial consequences</cite>, but <cite id="9ea234ab-2">low‑quality, symbolic disclosures raise concerns about credibility</cite>. 

# Background and definitions

Climate risk disclosure refers to reporting on material climate-related risks and opportunities that can affect financial performance and risk profiles, typically structured around frameworks like SASB, CDSB, GRI, TCFD, and increasingly ISSB/IFRS S1/S2. <cite id="9ea234ab-0">Regulators in several jurisdictions have moved from voluntary to mandatory alignment with TCFD and related frameworks, recognizing that voluntary disclosure is insufficiently consistent for systemic risk management</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-4">TCFD emphasizes governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets to integrate climate risks into core financial reporting and comparability</cite>. Financial reporting quality (FRQ) encompasses completeness, reliability, timeliness, and decision-usefulness of financial and nonfinancial information, often proxied by audit report quality, accrual quality, restatement risk, analyst forecast accuracy, and timely filings. 

# How widespread is climate risk disclosure in Sub‑Saharan Africa, and who adopts?

<cite id="64f34a72-0">Across SSA, nonfinancial disclosure has grown as firms pursue financing and investor access, but prior SSA studies have not firmly established causal links between disclosure and improved financial reporting quality</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-1">A cross‑country panel of 2390 firm‑years across six SSA countries shows average Environmental Disclosure Index (EDI) of 24.57/100, with large standard deviation (26.03), meaning many firms disclose minimally while others engage more comprehensively</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-1">Specifically, carbon emissions disclosures appear in 38.2% of firms, water usage in 40.3%, occupational hazard disclosures in 27.3%, and regulatory compliance disclosures in 14.1%, underscoring uneven coverage of critical risk areas</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-0">Board characteristics and ownership structure correlate with ESG disclosure intensity in SSA, consistent with governance as a driver of adoption</cite>. 

South Africa’s JSE provides the clearest enforced pathway. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Content analyses show that integrated reporting in South Africa increased disclosure of human, social/relationship, natural, and intellectual capital relative to pre‑mandate periods</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Studies of top JSE firms find that integrated reporting quality is associated with better accounting performance, implying improved information environments</cite>. On climate specifically, <cite id="cea1a99e-3">carbon disclosure has been mandated through King III/IV and JSE rules, with firms disclosing emissions to signal compliance and legitimacy</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-1">Recent alignment with IFRS S1/S2 (effective 2024) raises the bar for decision‑useful sustainability and climate information and has been accompanied by measurable improvements in the quality and thematic depth of climate-related disclosures among JSE Top‑40 firms</cite>. 

These patterns suggest both regulatory push and firm-level pull: <cite id="64f34a72-0">ownership/governance structures and stakeholder pressures increase adoption</cite>, and <cite id="cea1a99e-3">legitimacy concerns motivate disclosure in emerging markets with investor perceptions of climate reporting as critical</cite>. 

# Do climate risk disclosures improve financial reporting quality?

Direct SSA-wide causal estimates on accrual/audit/restatement quality are scarce, but multiple strands suggest improvements where disclosure is enforced and credible:

- South Africa/JSE evidence: <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Mandatory integrated reporting increased disclosure breadth and quality of nonfinancial capitals, and higher integrated reporting scores co‑moved with better accounting performance</cite>, consistent with improved information usefulness. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Analyses document significantly larger increases in social/relationship and human capital disclosures after the mandate, indicating a measurable improvement in the information environment</cite>. Although these studies proxy FRQ via performance and disclosure quality rather than audit/accrual metrics, they imply that standardized, mandated narratives and disclosures enhance decision‑usefulness. On climate specifically, <cite id="cea1a99e-3">South Africa’s King III/IV embed carbon disclosures in annual reporting and justify financial performance links through legitimacy channels</cite>, indicating that credible emissions reporting can credibly reduce information asymmetries for capital providers.

- Global/EM syntheses: <cite id="9ea234ab-2">A structured review of 134 empirical studies finds that climate disclosure quality and extent are associated with financial implications, including capital market outcomes and cost of capital, but also warns of symbolic reporting and greenwashing when disclosure quality is low</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-0">Convergence with TCFD and alignment with ISSB/IFRS S2 are intended to raise comparability and decision‑usefulness, addressing earlier fragmentation that reduced effectiveness</cite>. This supports the mechanism that well‑structured, financially material climate disclosures can improve FRQ by reducing asymmetries and aligning forward‑looking risk context with financial statements.

- Readiness and capacity constraints: <cite id="64f34a72-4">Despite voluntary and mandatory initiatives, SSA firms face gaps in consistency, comparability, and quality due to limited technical expertise and weak enforcement</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">Where alignment with TCFD/ISSB is shallow, disclosure may not reliably reflect underlying risk management or performance, blunting FRQ benefits</cite>. Thus, adoption quality matters: standardized frameworks and assurance capacity are necessary for FRQ gains to materialize.

Title: Quality, determinants and financial consequences of climate change disclosures: a structured review
Snippet: this study presents a structured review of empirical research on climate change disclosure, analyzing 134 articles published in journals ranked 2 or higher according to the aBS 2024 journal ranking, spanning from January 2010 to January 2025. Following the implementation of the Paris agreement in 2016 and the release of the tcFD recommendations in 2017, companies have been facing growing pressure to disclose information on climate-related risks and opportunities, driven by global efforts to limit warming. we also noticed a notable rise in related research, especially during the last two years 2023-2024. the review synthesizes findings on different themes related to climate reporting, e.g. the characteristics of climate disclosures, the quality and extent of reporting, determinants of climate reporting, financial implications and issues such as greenwashing allegations and legitimacy concerns. 

this structured review contributes to the existing literature by examining both climate risks/carbon disclosures based on cDP, and climate-related risks and opportunities disclosures guided by the tcFD recommendations. Prior literature research has concentrated on carbon disclosure alone ignoring climate-related disclosures based on tcFD recommendations (e.g. alam & costa, 2025;Borghei, 2021;Shui et al., 2023;wang, 2023). Recognizing the limitations of previous reviews, this review expands the analysis by incorporating climate change disclosures based on both cDP and tcFD recommendations. Furthermore, the scope of this review extends beyond previous studies by adding a broader array of themes. it notably addresses the historical evolution of climate change disclosures, characteristics of climate disclosures, quality of climate reporting and the determinants climate reporting, and explores the critical issue of greenwashing, explicitly linking it to disclosure quality. this thematic integration has not been covered in prior literature reviews. Moreover, this review covers high-impact articles indexed in the aBS journal guide 2024. 

the structured review identified several critical insights regarding climate change disclosures. First, there are efforts toward convergence in climate reporting standards, particularly driven by frameworks, such as the tcFD and iFRS S2; however, global standardization remains incomplete due to differing regional practices and regulatory contexts. additionally, while climate disclosures are increasing, their effectiveness in reflecting actual environmental performance is mixed, raising concerns about symbolic reporting and greenwashing.
</snippet>

Title: Repurposing the use of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework for South Africa’s public sector
Snippet: This research systematically reviewed academic and grey literature on the potential of the TCFD framework to promote climaterelated disclosure in the public sector of South Africa, as shown in Figure 1. A document search for scholarly work was conducted in the Scopus and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by a general Internet search for authoritative documents and reports from governments and organizations, such as the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the African Development Bank. The Scopus and Google Scholar databases were preferred over other indexes due to their potential to combat predatory publishing and protect the integrity of the scholarly record. The authors entered the following keywords: TCFD, climate-risk disclosures, and South Africa, using Boolean combinations, for the period from 2015 to the present. The period from 2015 onwards was chosen because 2015 was the year when the TCFD was established by the Financial Stability Board (FSB) to promote climate-related disclosures of financial risks and opportunities, initially focusing on private sector entities. 

The authors identified more than 1000 documents from both databases and other sources related to this review. The initial search yielded 357 articles from the Scopus and Google Scholar databases, while 19 documents were obtained from other sources. The authors examined discrepancies and reached a consensus on the final inclusion. After removing duplicates and final selection, 32 articles met the inclusion criteria in this systematic review after applying the inclusion selection criteria (kindly note Table 1). During the review process, 79 documents were selected based on title screening, while abstract screening obtained a total of 52 documents. 

The main limitation encountered by the authors during the review process was that the Scopus database did not fully address the TCFD as it is implemented in South Africa, but focused more on sustainability reporting and climate disclosures in general. The Google Scholar database and authoritative documents published by other credible organisations mitigated the limitation.
</snippet>

Title: Conceptual perspectives on climate risk disclosures for businesses and public sector
Snippet: Climate-related financial disclosures have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their potential to reduce information asymmetries, enable risk-informed investment, and strengthen market and financial system stability (Edwards et al. 2020). Carney (2015) emphasized the need for improved transparency and disclosure of climate risks to allow investors to make more informed decisions. Since then, several climate risk disclosure frameworks have emerged, each with its own focus and strengths. 

The most prominent of these include the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), the Climate Disclosure Standards Board (CDSB), the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), and the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). While the GRI and CDSB emphasize sustainability and environmental performance, and SASB focuses on sector-specific financial materiality, the TCFD distinguishes itself by providing a standardized framework to promote alignment across different jurisdictions and existing regimes (TCFD 2023). The TCFD, established by the Financial Stability Board in 2015, represents a step-change in climate disclosure by targeting how climate risks, both physical and transition, affect financial outcomes and institutional stability. Its recommendations are structured around four key themes: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets (TCFD 2017). This structure supports consistency and comparability across firms and sectors, while encouraging forward-looking scenario analysis. Unlike many earlier frameworks, the TCFD is designed specifically to integrate climate risk into core corporate governance and financial reporting practices. 

The strength of the TCFD framework is enhanced by its increasing global uptake and regulatory integration. Countries such as the UK, New Zealand, and members of the EU have incorporated TCFD principles into mandatory disclosure legislation. Its emphasis on financially material, decision-useful information has made it more appealing to investors and regulators, although this focus on measurable risks may overlook complex or longerterm climate threats that resist easy quantification. The TCFD has also become a foundational model for international harmonization efforts, with the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) explicitly building on its recommendations to establish a global baseline for climate-related financial disclosures (Australian Government, The Treasury 2022).

# Executive summary

There is persuasive SSA evidence that climate risk disclosure has been expanding and is associated with stronger governance and nonfinancial transparency, but direct causal estimates of improved financial reporting quality (FRQ) for Sub‑Saharan African non‑financial firms remain limited and uneven. <cite id="64f34a72-0">Across SSA, ESG/climate disclosure has grown in response to investor stakeholder demands and access-to-capital incentives, yet empirical confirmation of its impacts on reporting quality has been thin</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-1">A multi-country SSA sample shows substantial heterogeneity in environmental disclosure quality, with average Environmental Disclosure Index scores around a quarter of a full scale and only partial coverage of core risk indicators such as carbon emissions and regulatory compliance</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">In South Africa, JSE-mandated integrated reporting increased disclosure of human, social/relationship, natural, and intellectual capital and improved integrated reporting quality over time</cite>, <cite id="cea1a99e-2">with studies documenting greater disclosure breadth and positive associations between higher integrated reporting scores and better accounting performance</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-3">Carbon and climate-related disclosures have also been embedded into annual reporting requirements via King III/IV and JSE rules, with research motivated by the expectation that such disclosures affect financial outcomes through legitimacy channels</cite>. 

On effects and selection: <cite id="9ea234ab-2">A structured review of 134 empirical articles finds that climate disclosure quality and determinants are linked to financial implications, but also flags concerns about symbolic reporting and greenwashing</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">It documents rising convergence with TCFD and IFRS S2, yet emphasizes that effectiveness in reflecting underlying performance is mixed</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-4">Recent assessments of readiness for IFRS S1/S2 in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa highlight persistent gaps in consistency, comparability, and quality, with capacity and enforcement constraints as key barriers</cite>. Put together, the balance of evidence suggests that adoption of climate risk disclosure in SSA is associated with measurable improvements in reporting transparency and quality where enforced (e.g., South Africa), and that higher-quality reporters are more likely to adopt due to governance and legitimacy incentives; however, robust SSA‑specific causal estimates on financial accounting quality (e.g., accrual quality, restatements, audit report quality) are scarce, and symbolic or greenwashing risks can mute or reverse benefits if capacity and assurance mechanisms are weak. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">Where disclosure is high‑quality and decision‑useful, studies report positive financial consequences</cite>, but <cite id="9ea234ab-2">low‑quality, symbolic disclosures raise concerns about credibility</cite>. 

# Background and definitions

Climate risk disclosure refers to reporting on material climate-related risks and opportunities that can affect financial performance and risk profiles, typically structured around frameworks like SASB, CDSB, GRI, TCFD, and increasingly ISSB/IFRS S1/S2. <cite id="9ea234ab-0">Regulators in several jurisdictions have moved from voluntary to mandatory alignment with TCFD and related frameworks, recognizing that voluntary disclosure is insufficiently consistent for systemic risk management</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-4">TCFD emphasizes governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets to integrate climate risks into core financial reporting and comparability</cite>. Financial reporting quality (FRQ) encompasses completeness, reliability, timeliness, and decision-usefulness of financial and nonfinancial information, often proxied by audit report quality, accrual quality, restatement risk, analyst forecast accuracy, and timely filings. 

# How widespread is climate risk disclosure in Sub‑Saharan Africa, and who adopts?

<cite id="64f34a72-0">Across SSA, nonfinancial disclosure has grown as firms pursue financing and investor access, but prior SSA studies have not firmly established causal links between disclosure and improved financial reporting quality</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-1">A cross‑country panel of 2390 firm‑years across six SSA countries shows average Environmental Disclosure Index (EDI) of 24.57/100, with large standard deviation (26.03), meaning many firms disclose minimally while others engage more comprehensively</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-1">Specifically, carbon emissions disclosures appear in 38.2% of firms, water usage in 40.3%, occupational hazard disclosures in 27.3%, and regulatory compliance disclosures in 14.1%, underscoring uneven coverage of critical risk areas</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-0">Board characteristics and ownership structure correlate with ESG disclosure intensity in SSA, consistent with governance as a driver of adoption</cite>. 

South Africa’s JSE provides the clearest enforced pathway. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Content analyses show that integrated reporting in South Africa increased disclosure of human, social/relationship, natural, and intellectual capital relative to pre‑mandate periods</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Studies of top JSE firms find that integrated reporting quality is associated with better accounting performance, implying improved information environments</cite>. On climate specifically, <cite id="cea1a99e-3">carbon disclosure has been mandated through King III/IV and JSE rules, with firms disclosing emissions to signal compliance and legitimacy</cite>. <cite id="cea1a99e-1">Recent alignment with IFRS S1/S2 (effective 2024) raises the bar for decision‑useful sustainability and climate information and has been accompanied by measurable improvements in the quality and thematic depth of climate-related disclosures among JSE Top‑40 firms</cite>. 

These patterns suggest both regulatory push and firm-level pull: <cite id="64f34a72-0">ownership/governance structures and stakeholder pressures increase adoption</cite>, and <cite id="cea1a99e-3">legitimacy concerns motivate disclosure in emerging markets with investor perceptions of climate reporting as critical</cite>. 

# Do climate risk disclosures improve financial reporting quality?

Direct SSA-wide causal estimates on accrual/audit/restatement quality are scarce, but multiple strands suggest improvements where disclosure is enforced and credible:

- South Africa/JSE evidence: <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Mandatory integrated reporting increased disclosure breadth and quality of nonfinancial capitals, and higher integrated reporting scores co‑moved with better accounting performance</cite>, consistent with improved information usefulness. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Analyses document significantly larger increases in social/relationship and human capital disclosures after the mandate, indicating a measurable improvement in the information environment</cite>. Although these studies proxy FRQ via performance and disclosure quality rather than audit/accrual metrics, they imply that standardized, mandated narratives and disclosures enhance decision‑usefulness. On climate specifically, <cite id="cea1a99e-3">South Africa’s King III/IV embed carbon disclosures in annual reporting and justify financial performance links through legitimacy channels</cite>, indicating that credible emissions reporting can credibly reduce information asymmetries for capital providers.

- Global/EM syntheses: <cite id="9ea234ab-2">A structured review of 134 empirical studies finds that climate disclosure quality and extent are associated with financial implications, including capital market outcomes and cost of capital, but also warns of symbolic reporting and greenwashing when disclosure quality is low</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-0">Convergence with TCFD and alignment with ISSB/IFRS S2 are intended to raise comparability and decision‑usefulness, addressing earlier fragmentation that reduced effectiveness</cite>. This supports the mechanism that well‑structured, financially material climate disclosures can improve FRQ by reducing asymmetries and aligning forward‑looking risk context with financial statements.

- Readiness and capacity constraints: <cite id="64f34a72-4">Despite voluntary and mandatory initiatives, SSA firms face gaps in consistency, comparability, and quality due to limited technical expertise and weak enforcement</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">Where alignment with TCFD/ISSB is shallow, disclosure may not reliably reflect underlying risk management or performance, blunting FRQ benefits</cite>. Thus, adoption quality matters: standardized frameworks and assurance capacity are necessary for FRQ gains to materialize.

Taken together, the SSA evidence base indicates that where climate risk disclosure is mandated or strongly institutionalized (e.g., South Africa), firms’ reporting environments improve in measurable, decision‑useful ways; and broader EM/global evidence shows that higher‑quality, TCFD‑aligned disclosures are associated with positive financial consequences, while low‑quality disclosures risk greenwashing and muted effects. <cite id="cea1a99e-2">Improved integrated reporting disclosures and performance in South Africa</cite> and <cite id="9ea234ab-2">positive financial implications linked to higher-quality climate disclosure</cite> support the causal pathway that climate risk disclosure can enhance FRQ, contingent on implementation quality and institutional support. 

# Self-selection versus causal improvement: who adopts, and why?

Adoption is not uniform and is correlated with governance and capacity:

- Governance-driven selection: <cite id="64f34a72-0">Board independence, gender diversity, and financial expertise are associated with greater sustainability reporting among SSA firms, while concentrated block ownership can hinder transparency</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-1">High block ownership averages 54.75% across 239 SSA listed firms, suggesting influence that may promote or impede disclosure depending on stakeholder alignment</cite>. These findings imply that higher-quality reporting firms—characterized by stronger governance—are more likely to adopt climate disclosure, at least in part due to self-selection.

- Legitimacy and investor demand: <cite id="cea1a99e-3">In South Africa, firms disclose carbon emissions to signal compliance and sustain legitimacy in the eyes of investors and capital providers</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-0">Firms recognize that nonfinancial disclosure improves access to funding and builds trust, motivating adoption among higher-quality reporters</cite>. 

- Quality and credibility caveats: <cite id="64f34a72-4">However, readiness assessments find inconsistent and incomplete climate disclosures across Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa, with capacity and enforcement gaps undermining decision-usefulness</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">A structured review documents greenwashing concerns when disclosure quality is low, reinforcing that adoption without capability leads to symbolic reporting, which does not improve FRQ</cite>. 

Overall, available SSA evidence is consistent with both mechanisms operating simultaneously: (i) higher baseline reporting quality firms self-select into climate disclosure via governance and stakeholder incentives; and (ii) in jurisdictions with strong mandates and assurance, adoption causally improves the quality and usefulness of reporting. Distinguishing these mechanisms requires quasi-experimental designs (e.g., mandate shocks, listing upgrades) paired with FRQ outcomes like restatement risk, accrual quality, and audit signals—of which SSA has limited but growing exemplars in the South African context. 

# Mechanisms and heterogeneity: why effects differ across SSA

- Framework alignment and assurance: <cite id="9ea234ab-0">TCFD’s governance/strategy/risk-management/metrics structure and increasing regulatory integration raise comparability and decision-usefulness</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">Convergence with ISSB/IFRS S1/S2 is associated with better-aligned, financially material disclosures and documented links to financial consequences</cite>. In SSA, where frameworks have historically varied, alignment reduces ambiguity and enhances the informational role of nonfinancial statements.

- Governance and sectoral context: <cite id="64f34a72-0">Board expertise and independence increase sustainability reporting intensity</cite>, while concentrated ownership can dampen transparency, implying heterogeneous adoption and impact across corporate governance structures. In energy-intensive sectors, <cite id="64f34a72-3">stakeholder pressure and sectoral relevance amplify the value of environmental and climate obligations disclosure</cite>.

- Capacity and enforcement: <cite id="64f34a72-4">Limited technical expertise and weak enforcement hinder consistent, high-quality climate accounting, reducing the likelihood that adoption translates into measurable FRQ gains</cite>. South Africa’s regulatory stack (King III/IV, JSE rules, and recent ISSB alignment) provides stronger assurance backstops than many SSA peers, plausibly magnifying FRQ benefits.

# Evidence gaps and what would resolve them

Two gaps limit firm conclusions for SSA non-financial firms:

1) Causal FRQ estimates: There are few SSA-wide studies linking climate risk adoption to hard FRQ metrics (e.g., restatements, accrual quality, audit report quality, analyst forecast accuracy). <cite id="64f34a72-0">Existing SSA work documents determinants and rising disclosure</cite>, and <cite id="cea1a99e-2">South Africa shows improved integrated reporting and performance associations</cite>, but direct accrual/audit evidence is sparse. A quasi-experimental design exploiting staggered adoption of TCFD/SASB/IFRS S2 across SSA exchanges, or the 2024 IFRS S2 effective date in listed firms, paired with external assurance requirements, would cleanly identify causal effects on restatement risk and earnings management.

2) Self-selection tests: While governance correlates with adoption, tests that disentangle endogeneity (e.g., instrumental variables based on jurisdictional mandate timing, listing lotteries, or auditor adoption shocks; Heckman selection models) are limited in SSA. <cite id="64f34a72-0">Observational evidence suggests governance-driven adoption</cite> and <cite id="cea1a99e-3">legitimacy-driven adoption</cite>, but identification is needed to quantify the share of adoption due to self-selection versus improvements induced by mandates.

# Practical implications for SSA policymakers and firms

- Mandates and alignment: <cite id="cea1a99e-2">South Africa’s experience indicates that mandated integrated and climate disclosures measurably raise disclosure quality and are associated with better financial outcomes</cite>. SSA regulators can emulate this by strengthening listing and exchange requirements (e.g., structured climate risk narratives with governance, risk management, and metrics/targets aligned to TCFD/ISSB), coupled with assurance and enforcement.

- Governance and capacity building: <cite id="64f34a72-0">Investing in board expertise and independence, and limiting concentrated block ownership, improves both climate disclosure and overall reporting quality</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-4">Capacity programs in carbon accounting, GHG measurement, and assurance, plus penalties for noncompliance, address readiness gaps that otherwise lead to symbolic reporting</cite>.

- Risk of symbolic disclosure: <cite id="9ea234ab-2">Firms should focus on high-quality, decision-useful climate disclosures aligned with TCFD/ISSB to avoid greenwashing and to realize FRQ benefits; low-quality disclosures are unlikely to improve capital market efficiency and may erode trust</cite>.

# Bottom line

<cite id="64f34a72-0">Adoption of climate risk disclosure is rising in SSA and is linked to stronger governance and stakeholder trust</cite>, and <cite id="cea1a99e-2">in South Africa, mandated integrated and climate disclosures have improved the quality and breadth of reported information and are associated with better financial outcomes</cite>. <cite id="9ea234ab-2">Across markets, higher-quality, TCFD-aligned climate disclosures are associated with positive financial consequences, but low-quality disclosures risk greenwashing and muted effects</cite>. <cite id="64f34a72-4">Given SSA capacity and enforcement constraints, the causal improvement in financial reporting quality depends critically on the quality of implementation and assurance</cite>. In short, climate risk disclosure can improve SSA firms’ reporting quality when embedded in strong governance and aligned to standardized, auditable frameworks; otherwise, higher-quality reporters self-select into disclosure while low-quality adoption may merely signal compliance without substantive FRQ gains. <cite id="64f34a72-0">Further SSA-specific causal studies using quasi-experimental designs and FRQ metrics are needed to quantify effects and self-selection more precisely</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Evidence of the impact of corporate governance on ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa: the moderating role of ownership structure
Snippet: Despite a significant cultural and socioeconomic difference, little is understood about the interaction of cultural and social contexts with reporting, beyond the images of extreme poverty repeatedly documented in the media (Waweru 2020). However, there is a paucity of studies on the impact of corporate governance on ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). To the best of our knowledge, the only available studies are Waweru (2020), which analyses the disclosure of business ethics and corporate governance in sub-Saharan Africa, together with Githaiga and Kosgei (2023), that examined the board characteristics and sustainability reporting of selected firms from countries in East Africa. Nonetheless, ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa has gained traction as companies recognise the need to address ESG concerns, with the aim of creating value, building trust and contributing to solving significant challenges (Tilt et al. 2021). 

In terms of companies in sub-Saharan Africa, enhanced ESG disclosure practices are crucial to access funding sources and attract investors (Siueia et al. 2019). Improved corporate disclosure practices, including non-financial disclosures, are becoming increasingly influential as stakeholders demand transparency and accountability (e.g. Amran & Keat Ooi 2014;Maas & Sampers 2020). However, recent studies focusing on sub-Saharan Africa have not yet confirmed this evidence. Notably, Githaiga and Kosgei (2023), examined the correlation between the board characteristics and sustainability reporting of listed firms in East Africa. The findings they obtained underlined that board gender diversity, board financial expertise and board independence are positively and significantly associated with sustainability reporting, whereas board size has a negative and significant effect on sustainability reporting. Similarly, Ofoegbu et al. (2018) examined corporate board characteristics and environmental disclosure quantity based on South Africa (integrated reporting) and Nigeria (traditional reporting). The authors determined a significant positive relationship between board independence and environmental disclosure in Nigeria. The research they conducted focused on individual nations or a specific economic bloc. Given that the sub-Saharan region comprises the largest part of the continent, the understanding derived from these particular studies has substantial implications not only for the entire region of Africa, but also for other emerging economies that share similar developmental characteristics.

Title: Block ownership as a moderator in the relationship between environmental risk disclosures and environmental reporting transparency in Sub Saharan Africa
Snippet: Table 4 presents summary statistics for 2390 firm-year observations drawn from 239 non-financial listed firms across six Sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries. The results highlight considerable variation in corporate environmental transparency within the region. The mean score on the Environmental Disclosure Index (EDI) is 24.57 out of 100, indicating that, on average, firms disclose only a quarter of the expected environmental information. The high standard deviation (26.03) further suggests substantial heterogeneity across firms while some engage in relatively comprehensive reporting, many provide minimal or no environmental disclosure. 

The average rates of disclosure across the four environmental risk indicators are generally low. Specifically, carbon emissions disclosures (EMMID) are reported by 38.2% of firms, while 40.3% disclose water usage (WATD). Occupational hazard disclosures (OCCHAZ) are found in only 27.3% of cases, and compliance with environmental regulations (CLRD) is reported by just 14.1% of firms. These figures underscore significant gaps in transparency, particularly in regulatory compliance and workplace safety areas that are critical for environmental accountability and stakeholder assurance. 

In terms of governance structure, block ownership (BLOWN), defined as shareholding exceeding 5% by individual or institutional investors, averages 54.75%, suggesting a high concentration of ownership. This concentration may exert significant influence on corporate reporting strategies, either to promote or hinder transparency. The sample firms are largely mature, with an average incorporation year of 1986 (approximately 39 years of age). Board size varies considerably, with an average of nearly 10 directors, reflecting diversity in governance structures across the firms. 

Leverage, measured as the ratio of total liabilities to total assets multiplied by 100, has a mean value of 52.94, indicating that, on average, over half of firm assets are financed through debt. This reinforces the need to consider financial structure as a control variable in explaining environmental disclosure behaviour. Firm size, measured as the natural log of total assets, averages 20.85, indicating that the typical firm in our sample holds assets valued around US$1.05 billion. This reflects the inclusion of large listed firms from sectors such as energy and manufacturing.

Title: Effectiveness of Corporate Governance Attributes on Disclosure of Non-Financial Information in Developing Economies
Snippet: Data was obtained from annual reports of 146 non-financial firms with all the required information on corporate governance and disclosure, from selected Securities Exchanges in Sub-Saharan Africa, for the period 2013-2016. The choice of the period is justified because; for South African listed firms, this was a period during which the King III Report that came into effect in 2010, was being implemented. The Report outlines the application of several corporate governance attributes which were the focus of this study. The period was also when most companies globally were recovering from 2007-2010 financial crises which also affected some of the developing economies like Nigeria. It was expected that by this study period (2013)(2014)(2015)(2016), companies would have strengthened corporate governance systems to monitor operations and improve disclosure of all corporate information in order to boost investments and economic growth. The annual reports were for 95 companies listed on the Johannesburg Securities Exchange in South Africa, 25 companies listed on the Nigeria Stock Exchange in West Africa and 26 companies listed on the Nairobi and Uganda Securities Exchanges in East Africa. Financial firms such as banks and insurance companies were excluded from the study because they are specialised in nature with a tight regulatory environment and are normally subjected to different disclosure requirements and accounting principles (Abdifatah, 2013). The sample also excluded firms whose corporate governance data and information on corporate disclosure could not be obtained from the company websites, corporate governance reports and annual reports for the full period of the study. Most annual reports of companies listed on the selected Securities Exchanges in Sub-Saharan Africa are available from the BFA McGregor and Bloomberg Databases. These were the major sources of data for this study.

Title: Firm-specific characteristics and environmental disclosure of energy firms in Sub-Saharan Africa
Snippet: Amidst the vast and diverse landscapes of sub-Saharan Africa, the energy sector has emerged as a powerful catalyst driving economic progress and development, energizing industries, homes, and communities alike. However, this relentless growth in energy demand, propelled by a burgeoning population and expanding economies, comes hand in hand with an equally pressing challenge: environmental sustainability. 

In 2021, environmental sustainability took center stage as over 40,000 people, including 120 world leaders, 22,274 party delegates, 14,124 observers, and 3,886 media representatives, gathered in Glasgow, Scotland for the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP26). The event spanned two weeks and captivated global attention, with evidence, solutions, political will to act, and concrete signals of climate change action at the forefront of discussions (UN, 2021). Environmental disclosure has emerged as a crucial instrument at this critical juncture to address climate change and its consequences, offering valuable insights into corporate responsibility and transparency. 

Environmental disclosure can be considered critical for fostering stakeholder engagement and driving the "greening" of corporate financial reports. Tukur, Shehu, Mammadi, and Sulaiman (2019) stated that a firm can carry out corporate social responsibility by involving environmental conservation and sustainability activities. According to Nweze and Nwadialor (2020), environmental disclosure entails disclosing expenses incurred by a company to preserve and enhance its local environment in its annual report. In doing so, firms become more transparent about their investments in environmental protection, particularly when these expenditures are linked to operations that negatively impact the natural world. 

In light of this, Jeroh (2020) highlights the significance of listed firms in sub-Saharan Africa, especially those in the energy industry, reporting their environmental obligations to the public. Failure to do so may hinder transparency, accountability, and the acquisition of legitimacy and recognition from stakeholders. This has prompted numerous studies underlining the need for better environmental performance, disclosure standards, and further recommendations for businesses to adopt eco-friendly practices. Environmental disclosure has emerged as a central discourse in accounting literature because of the mounting pressure to fulfill many environmental obligations across various industries. 

Regrettably, despite the increasing emphasis on environmental sustainability, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the factors influencing environmental disclosure practices among sub-Saharan African energy firms.

Title: Carbon Accounting and Corporate Disclosure: Assessing the Readiness of Listed Firms for Global Sustainability Standards (ISSB/IFRS S1 & S2) in Ghana and Comparative Insights from Nigeria and South Africa.
Snippet: Global concerns about climate change, environmental degradation, and sustainability performance have resulted in calls for increased corporate transparency and accountability. Adams and Abhayawansa (2022) testify that in response, the IFRS Foundation established the International Sustainability Standards Board in 2021 with the ambition of developing a comprehensive global baseline for sustainability reporting. The publication of IFRS S1, General Requirements for Sustainability-related Financial Disclosures, and IFRS S2, Climate-related Disclosures, in June 2023 constitutes a milestone in progress toward integration of ESG factors into mainstream financial reporting. IFRS Foundation (2023) Sustainability reporting practices are still fledgling in developing economies like Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa, though many firms have been disclosing environmental and social information on a voluntary basis. There remains a significant gap between such disclosures with respect to their consistency, comparability, and quality (Agyemang & Ansong, 2023; Dissanayake, 2024). Carbon accounting, particularly that involving the identification, quantification, and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions, remains underdeveloped in sub-Saharan Africa. Limited technical expertise, resource constraints, and weak enforcement of regulations impede the systemic adoption of sustainability frameworks. This study seeks to assess the readiness of listed firms in Ghana to implement IFRS S1 and S2, focusing on carbon-related disclosures as a proxy for climate reporting preparedness. It further places Ghana's readiness in a regional context by comparing it with the level of readiness of Nigeria and South Africa. The study combines content analysis of firm reports for the period 2018-2024 with a survey of accounting professionals in providing an evidence-based evaluation of Africa's preparedness for the ISSB standards.

snippet.text:
Amidst the vast and diverse landscapes of sub-Saharan Africa, the energy sector has emerged as a powerful catalyst driving economic progress and development, energizing industries, homes, and communities alike. However, this relentless growth in energy demand, propelled by a burgeoning population and expanding economies, comes hand in hand with an equally pressing challenge: environmental sustainability. 

In 2021, environmental sustainability took center stage as over 40,000 people, including 120 world leaders, 22,274 party delegates, 14,124 observers, and 3,886 media representatives, gathered in Glasgow, Scotland for the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP26). The event spanned two weeks and captivated global attention, with evidence, solutions, political will to act, and concrete signals of climate change action at the forefront of discussions (UN, 2021). Environmental disclosure has emerged as a crucial instrument at this critical juncture to address climate change and its consequences, offering valuable insights into corporate responsibility and transparency. 

Environmental disclosure can be considered critical for fostering stakeholder engagement and driving the "greening" of corporate financial reports. Tukur, Shehu, Mammadi, and Sulaiman (2019) stated that a firm can carry out corporate social responsibility by involving environmental conservation and sustainability activities. According to Nweze and Nwadialor (2020), environmental disclosure entails disclosing expenses incurred by a company to preserve and enhance its local environment in its annual report. In doing so, firms become more transparent about their investments in environmental protection, particularly when these expenditures are linked to operations that negatively impact the natural world. 

In light of this, Jeroh (2020) highlights the significance of listed firms in sub-Saharan Africa, especially those in the energy industry, reporting their environmental obligations to the public. Failure to do so may hinder transparency, accountability, and the acquisition of legitimacy and recognition from stakeholders. This has prompted numerous studies underlining the need for better environmental performance, disclosure standards, and further recommendations for businesses to adopt eco-friendly practices. Environmental disclosure has emerged as a central discourse in accounting literature because of the mounting pressure to fulfill many environmental obligations across various industries. 

Regrettably, despite the increasing emphasis on environmental sustainability, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the factors influencing environmental disclosure practices among sub-Saharan African energy firms.

snippet.text: Global concerns about climate change, environmental degradation, and sustainability performance have resulted in calls for increased corporate transparency and accountability. Adams and Abhayawansa (2022) testify that in response, the IFRS Foundation established the International Sustainability Standards Board in 2021 with the ambition of developing a comprehensive global baseline for sustainability reporting. The publication of IFRS S1, General Requirements for Sustainability-related Financial Disclosures, and IFRS S2, Climate-related Disclosures, in June 2023 constitutes a milestone in progress toward integration of ESG factors into mainstream financial reporting. IFRS Foundation (2023) Sustainability reporting practices are still fledgling in developing economies like Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa, though many firms have been disclosing environmental and social information on a voluntary basis. There remains a significant gap between such disclosures with respect to their consistency, comparability, and quality (Agyemang & Ansong, 2023; Dissanayake, 2024). Carbon accounting, particularly that involving the identification, quantification, and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions, remains underdeveloped in sub-Saharan Africa. Limited technical expertise, resource constraints, and weak enforcement of regulations impede the systemic adoption of sustainability frameworks. This study seeks to assess the readiness of listed firms in Ghana to implement IFRS S1 and S2, focusing on carbon-related disclosures as a proxy for climate reporting preparedness. It further places Ghana's readiness in a regional context by comparing it with the level of readiness of Nigeria and South Africa. The study combines content analysis of firm reports for the period 2018-2024 with a survey of accounting professionals in providing an evidence-based evaluation of Africa's preparedness for the ISSB standards.

Title: A comparative analysis of the IFRS prototype standard and current climate-related disclosures by FTSE/JSE financials 15 listed companies in South Africa
Snippet: No content available

Title: Climate Sentiment Analysis on the Disclosures of the Corporations Listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange
Snippet: The objective was to enhance the quality of sustainability reporting by aligning it to existing regulations pertaining to financial disclosures. On 26 June 2023, the ISSB released IFRS S1 and S2 that became effective from 1 January 2024. Companies are mandated to disclose decision-useful information regarding sustainability-related (IFRS S1) and climaterelated (IFRS S2) risks and opportunities that may affect their risk profiles (International Sustainability Standards Board, 2023a, 2023b). 

Sentiment extracted from climate-related publications produce interesting insights. Sources of climate risk sentiment include social media (Rosenberg et al., 2023;Upadhyaya et al., 2023;Uthirapathy & Sandanam, 2023); news sources (Faccini et al., 2023); or company financial reports (Bingler et al., 2022;Van der Lugt et al., 2025). 

In this study, climate-related sentiment data are extracted from the Financial Times to gauge sentiment based on recent global events (2024 to 2025). Next, the integrated and sustainability reports of the companies that make up the top 40 all-share index on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) were sourced. The JSE top 40 index consists of the largest 40 companies ranked by market value (JSE, 2020). The study considers how the climate-related sentiment has changed between 2010 and 2024 and the main themes that drive the change. The study demonstrates that the evolution of reporting standards has positively influenced climate-related disclosures, indicating that businesses are recognizing their climate-related risks and translating them into strategic actions. This study provides valuable insights for regulators, accounting professionals and investors regarding the current state of corporate disclosure and future actions needed in South Africa. 

Previous South African studies have established the impact of investor sentiment on the stock market, where investor sentiment is measured by market variables such as share turnover, equity issue ratio, rand/dollar bid-ask spread and interest rates (Moodley et al., 2025;Naidoo et al., 2025).

Title: Integrated Reporting and Firm Value in the Nigerian and South African Oil and Gas Sector
Snippet: Also, in terms of the stock market and accounting performance, firms with high integrated reporting performed better than firms with a low score for integrated reporting. Haji and Anifowose (2016) examined the trend in integrated reporting practice in South Africa as a result of the mandatory disclosure issued by the JSE. They concluded that there is an improvement in the quality of integrated reporting practices following the regulation, but that some firms are still not serious about the regulation. 

Similarly, Setia et al. (2015) examined integrated reporting in South Africa. Based on a sample size of the top 25 JSE listed companies from 2009-2012 and using content analysis, they analyzed the changes in the extent of disclosure of the various capital types using t-tests. They found that the introduction of integrated reporting in South Africa has resulted in an increase in the disclosure of human, social/relationship, natural, and intellectual capital information of the quoted companies. They, therefore, concluded that an increase in the disclosure of social and relationship capital is statistically and significantly greater than the increase in the disclosure of other capital types. Their findings indicate that the JSE-quoted companies are adopting a legitimate strategy based on symbolic management when preparing integrated reports. 

Additionally, Cosma et al. (2018) examined the effect of integrated reports on firm value in South Africa between 2013 and 2016. The study used stock return as a proxy for firm value, while the national market index return was used as a proxy for integrated reporting. The ordinary least square regression was used as a method of analysis. In this study, they found that integrated reporting had a positive effect on firm performance. As a result, they concluded that firm managers should increase their quality of integrated disclosure.

Title: The Effect of Mandatory Carbon Disclosure on Financial Performance: Evidence From South African Listed Carbon-Intensive Companies
Snippet: Additionally, comparatively little is known concerning this relationship within the African background in general and South Africa in particular. South Africa characterizes an exciting context for this kind of research. South Africa is among the twenty countries with the world's most significant greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (Ganda, 2018). As a result, South Africa is presently at the forefront in Africa to develop proactive tools to alleviate the risks of climate change. 

This study evolves around the King Code III and IV as developed in South Africa. In South Africa, carbon disclosure has been mandated to be part of annual reporting by the introduction of King III in 2009 and, recently, King IV. Globally, carbon disclosure is required by ISO 14064-1 (Lewandowski, 2017). Furthermore, the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) also demands that all listed companies extensively report on their environmental, economic and social activities in their annual reports. Thus, this makes carbon emission disclosure mandatory for all JSE-listed through the operation of King III and IV. Internationally, institutions such as Carbon Disclosure Project has been instrumental in commending companies for disclosing their climate change activities, such as carbon emissions. This is also vital because investors perceive climate risk reporting as critical as conventional reporting (Matsumura et al., 2014;Lee et al., 2015). This is important because reporting carbon emissions is "a newer area of environmental reporting" in emerging markets such as South Africa (Iriyadi & Antonio, 2021;Ganda, 2018). This partly explains the few studies on the nexus between carbon disclosure and finance in emerging markets. 

The study uses a legitimacy theory to describe carbon emissions disclosure about financial performance. Therefore, by performing carbon emissions disclosure, corporations try to persuade stakeholders by underlining that they comply with their expectations to sustain their legitimacy (Albarrak et al., 2019). This study is motivated by the call to understand King IV and CDP mandatory carbon emissions disclosure's impact on financial performance in an emerging market perspective. So, this research aims to examine the association between mandatory carbon disclosure and financial performance. Attaining this objective might validate how the effect of climate change on corporates' operations may be concurrently related to both the environment and business.

Title: JSE EFFICIENCY AND SHARE PRICE REACTION TO FORCED FINANCIAL RESTATEMENTS
Snippet: In providing an overview of accounting standards and JSE listing requirements, the literature review highlights some of the technical aspects and requirements relating to financial restatements. This is followed by a review of the restatement literature as well as research on market efficiency and the efficient market hypothesis (EMH). The literature review concludes by highlighting some of the achievements of the JSE and various aspects that may influence the efficiency of the JSE. Given that the South African literature on financial restatement is limited, the US literature is used predominantly to illustrate the impact of financial restatement on share prices.

documents.snippet:
The objective was to enhance the quality of sustainability reporting by aligning it to existing regulations pertaining to financial disclosures. On 26 June 2023, the ISSB released IFRS S1 and S2 that became effective from 1 January 2024. Companies are mandated to disclose decision-useful information regarding sustainability-related (IFRS S1) and climaterelated (IFRS S2) risks and opportunities that may affect their risk profiles (International Sustainability Standards Board, 2023a, 2023b). 

Sentiment extracted from climate-related publications produce interesting insights. Sources of climate risk sentiment include social media (Rosenberg et al., 2023;Upadhyaya et al., 2023;Uthirapathy & Sandanam, 2023); news sources (Faccini et al., 2023); or company financial reports (Bingler et al., 2022;Van der Lugt et al., 2025). 

In this study, climate-related sentiment data are extracted from the Financial Times to gauge sentiment based on recent global events (2024 to 2025). Next, the integrated and sustainability reports of the companies that make up the top 40 all-share index on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) were sourced. The JSE top 40 index consists of the largest 40 companies ranked by market value (JSE, 2020). The study considers how the climate-related sentiment has changed between 2010 and 2024 and the main themes that drive the change. The study demonstrates that the evolution of reporting standards has positively influenced climate-related disclosures, indicating that businesses are recognizing their climate-related risks and translating them into strategic actions. This study provides valuable insights for regulators, accounting professionals and investors regarding the current state of corporate disclosure and future actions needed in South Africa. 

Previous South African studies have established the impact of investor sentiment on the stock market, where investor sentiment is measured by market variables such as share turnover, equity issue ratio, rand/dollar bid-ask spread and interest rates (Moodley et al., 2025;Naidoo et al., 2025).

Also, in terms of the stock market and accounting performance, firms with high integrated reporting performed better than firms with a low score for integrated reporting. They concluded that there is an improvement in the quality of integrated reporting practices following the regulation, but that some firms are still not serious about the regulation. 

Similarly, Setia et al. (2015) examined integrated reporting in South Africa. Based on a sample size of the top 25 JSE listed companies from 2009-2012 and using content analysis, they analyzed the changes in the extent of disclosure of the various capital types using t-tests. They found that the introduction of integrated reporting in South Africa has resulted in an increase in the disclosure of human, social/relationship, natural, and intellectual capital information of the quoted companies. They, therefore, concluded that an increase in the disclosure of social and relationship capital is statistically and significantly greater than the increase in the disclosure of other capital types. Their findings indicate that the JSE-quoted companies are adopting a legitimate strategy based on symbolic management when preparing integrated reports. 

Additionally, Cosma et al. (2018) examined the effect of integrated reports on firm value in South Africa between 2013 and 2016. The study used stock return as a proxy for firm value, while the national market index return was used as a proxy for integrated reporting. The ordinary least square regression was used as a method of analysis. In this study, they found that integrated reporting had a positive effect on firm performance. As a result, they concluded that firm managers should increase their quality of integrated disclosure.

Title: Towards a conceptual framework for non-financial reporting inclusive of pandemic and climate risk reporting
Snippet: In most countries, companies with public debt or equity are obliged to disclose material information to the public. Material ESG risks such as climate-and pandemic-related risks arguably belong in that category (United States Government Accountability Office, 2020). Among different types of ESG risks, climaterelated risks are attracting the most attention. They have been ranked among the top long-term risks by impact and likelihood in the World Economic Forum's Global Risk Perception Survey (World Economic Forum, 2020a). Several other most likely and impactful long-term risks (e.g., biodiversity loss), according to this survey, are also linked to climate change. National regulators increasingly acknowledge that a voluntary approach to climate-related disclosure is not sufficient given the urgency of the climate threat (Her Majesty's Treasury, 2020;Shaw, 2020). 

Numerous regulations and frameworks exist on climate-related risk reporting, the most authoritative one being the recommendations of the TCFD. In 2019, the European Commission integrated the TCFD recommendations into its Guidelines on Climate-Related Information. The requirements in the legislation recently proposed by New Zealand and U.K. governments for disclosure of climate-related risk are intended to be aligned with the TCFD recommendations (Her Majesty's Treasury, 2020;Shaw, 2020). The TCFD implementation guide issued by SASB and CDSB shows that SASB's standards and CDSB's reporting framework can be used to provide disclosures aligned with the TCFD recommendation (CDSB and SASB, 2019). Corporate Reporting Dialog (2019a) provides guidance on using five of the most popular NFR frameworks (i.e., CDP, CDSB, GRI, IIRC and SASB) in a complementary manner with the TCFD recommendations. According to its 2020 report, there is almost complete alignment between the five NFR frameworks and the TCFD's principles and recommendations, and CDP, GRI, and SASB frameworks provide a high level of alignment with the TCFD's illustrative examples and metrics (Corporate Reporting Dialog, 2019a).

Title: KUALITAS PENGUNGKAPAN PELAPORAN IKLIM DENGAN REKOMENDASI TCFD PERUSAHAAN METAL-MINING DAN BANKS TAHUN 2020-2022
Snippet: Climate change has become a concern for every sector, including finance. This is the basis for the creation of the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations. This research aims to determine the quality of climate reporting disclosure following TCFD recommendations. The theories employed in this study are stakeholder theory and legitimacy theory. The content analysis method is utilized to understand and assess the quality of climate reporting disclosure from 18 companies during the period 2020-2022. The results indicate that the majority of companies achieve a moderate quality, suggesting that the implementation of TCFD recommendations is still considered sufficient. The main category of governance and the sub-category of target usage receive the highest rankings, indicating that the disclosure in these categories and sub-categories aligns with TCFD recommendations. The banking sector attains high quality, even though its impact on climate change is not direct. South Africa obtains a high percentage, while the United Kingdom consistently experiences improvement each year.

Title: Quality, determinants and financial consequences of climate change disclosures: a structured review
Snippet: this study presents a structured review of empirical research on climate change disclosure, analyzing 134 articles published in journals ranked 2 or higher according to the aBS 2024 journal ranking, spanning from January 2010 to January 2025. Following the implementation of the Paris agreement in 2016 and the release of the tcFD recommendations in 2017, companies have been facing growing pressure to disclose information on climate-related risks and opportunities, driven by global efforts to limit warming. we also noticed a notable rise in related research, especially during the last two years 2023-2024. the review synthesizes findings on different themes related to climate reporting, e.g. the characteristics of climate disclosures, the quality and extent of reporting, determinants of climate reporting, financial implications and issues such as greenwashing allegations and legitimacy concerns. 

this structured review contributes to the existing literature by examining both climate risks/carbon disclosures based on cDP, and climate-related risks and opportunities disclosures guided by the tcFD recommendations. Prior literature research has concentrated on carbon disclosure alone ignoring climate-related disclosures based on tcFD recommendations (e.g. alam & costa, 2025;Borghei, 2021;Shui et al., 2023;wang, 2023). Recognizing the limitations of previous reviews, this review expands the analysis by incorporating climate change disclosures based on both cDP and tcFD recommendations. Furthermore, the scope of this review extends beyond previous studies by adding a broader array of themes. it notably addresses the historical evolution of climate change disclosures, characteristics of climate disclosures, quality of climate reporting and the determinants climate reporting, and explores the critical issue of greenwashing, explicitly linking it to disclosure quality. this thematic integration has not been covered in prior literature reviews. Moreover, this review covers high-impact articles indexed in the aBS journal guide 2024. 

the structured review identified several critical insights regarding climate change disclosures. First, there are efforts toward convergence in climate reporting standards, particularly driven by frameworks, such as the tcFD and iFRS S2; however, global standardization remains incomplete due to differing regional practices and regulatory contexts. additionally, while climate disclosures are increasing, their effectiveness in reflecting actual environmental performance is mixed, raising concerns about symbolic reporting and greenwashing.

Title: Repurposing the use of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework for South Africa’s public sector
Snippet: This research systematically reviewed academic and grey literature on the potential of the TCFD framework to promote climaterelated disclosure in the public sector of South Africa, as shown in Figure 1. A document search for scholarly work was conducted in the Scopus and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by a general Internet search for authoritative documents and reports from governments and organizations, such as the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the African Development Bank. The Scopus and Google Scholar databases were preferred over other indexes due to their potential to combat predatory publishing and protect the integrity of the scholarly record. The authors entered the following keywords: TCFD, climate-risk disclosures, and South Africa, using Boolean combinations, for the period from 2015 to the present. The period from 2015 onwards was chosen because 2015 was the year when the TCFD was established by the Financial Stability Board (FSB) to promote climate-related disclosures of financial risks and opportunities, initially focusing on private sector entities. 

The authors identified more than 1000 documents from both databases and other sources related to this review. The initial search yielded 357 articles from the Scopus and Google Scholar databases, while 19 documents were obtained from other sources. The authors examined discrepancies and reached a consensus on the final inclusion. After removing duplicates and final selection, 32 articles met the inclusion criteria in this systematic review after applying the inclusion selection criteria (kindly note Table 1). During the review process, 79 documents were selected based on title screening, while abstract screening obtained a total of 52 documents. 

The main limitation encountered by the authors during the review process was that the Scopus database did not fully address the TCFD as it is implemented in South Africa, but focused more on sustainability reporting and climate disclosures in general. The Google Scholar database and authoritative documents published by other credible organisations mitigated the limitation.

Title: Conceptual perspectives on climate risk disclosures for businesses and public sector
Snippet: Climate-related financial disclosures have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their potential to reduce information asymmetries, enable risk-informed investment, and strengthen market and financial system stability (Edwards et al. 2020). Carney (2015) emphasized the need for improved transparency and disclosure of climate risks to allow investors to make more informed decisions. Since then, several climate risk disclosure frameworks have emerged, each with its own focus and strengths. 

The most prominent of these include the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), the Climate Disclosure Standards Board (CDSB), the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), and the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). While the GRI and CDSB emphasize sustainability and environmental performance, and SASB focuses on sector-specific financial materiality, the TCFD distinguishes itself by providing a standardized framework to promote alignment across different jurisdictions and existing regimes (TCFD 2023). The TCFD, established by the Financial Stability Board in 2015, represents a step-change in climate disclosure by targeting how climate risks, both physical and transition, affect financial outcomes and institutional stability. Its recommendations are structured around four key themes: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets (TCFD 2017). This structure supports consistency and comparability across firms and sectors, while encouraging forward-looking scenario analysis. Unlike many earlier frameworks, the TCFD is designed specifically to integrate climate risk into core corporate governance and financial reporting practices. 

The strength of the TCFD framework is enhanced by its increasing global uptake and regulatory integration. Countries such as the UK, New Zealand, and members of the EU have incorporated TCFD principles into mandatory disclosure legislation. Its emphasis on financially material, decision-useful information has made it more appealing to investors and regulators, although this focus on measurable risks may overlook complex or longerterm climate threats that resist easy quantification. The TCFD has also become a foundational model for international harmonization efforts, with the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) explicitly building on its recommendations to establish a global baseline for climate-related financial disclosures (Australian Government, The Treasury 2022).
