documents.title: Quality, determinants and financial consequences of climate change disclosures: a structured review
documents.snippet:
this study presents a structured review of empirical research on climate change disclosure, analyzing 134 articles published in journals ranked 2 or higher according to the aBS 2024 journal ranking, spanning from January 2010 to January 2025. Following the implementation of the Paris agreement in 2016 and the release of the tcFD recommendations in 2017, companies have been facing growing pressure to disclose information on climate-related risks and opportunities, driven by global efforts to limit warming. we also noticed a notable rise in related research, especially during the last two years 2023-2024. the review synthesizes findings on different themes related to climate reporting, e.g. the characteristics of climate disclosures, the quality and extent of reporting, determinants of climate reporting, financial implications and issues such as greenwashing allegations and legitimacy concerns. 

this structured review contributes to the existing literature by examining both climate risks/carbon disclosures based on cDP, and climate-related risks and opportunities disclosures guided by the tcFD recommendations. Prior literature research has concentrated on carbon disclosure alone ignoring climate-related disclosures based on tcFD recommendations (e.g. alam & costa, 2025;Borghei, 2021;Shui et al., 2023;wang, 2023). Recognizing the limitations of previous reviews, this review expands the analysis by incorporating climate change disclosures based on both cDP and tcFD recommendations. Furthermore, the scope of this review extends beyond previous studies by adding a broader array of themes. it notably addresses the historical evolution of climate change disclosures, characteristics of climate disclosures, quality of climate reporting and the determinants climate reporting, and explores the critical issue of greenwashing, explicitly linking it to disclosure quality. this thematic integration has not been covered in prior literature reviews. Moreover, this review covers high-impact articles indexed in the aBS journal guide 2024. 

the structured review identified several critical insights regarding climate change disclosures. First, there are efforts toward convergence in climate reporting standards, particularly driven by frameworks, such as the tcFD and iFRS S2; however, global standardization remains incomplete due to differing regional practices and regulatory contexts. additionally, while climate disclosures are increasing, their effectiveness in reflecting actual environmental performance is mixed, raising concerns about symbolic reporting and greenwashing.

documents.title: Repurposing the use of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework for South Africa’s public sector
documents.snippet:
This research systematically reviewed academic and grey literature on the potential of the TCFD framework to promote climaterelated disclosure in the public sector of South Africa, as shown in Figure 1. A document search for scholarly work was conducted in the Scopus and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by a general Internet search for authoritative documents and reports from governments and organizations, such as the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the African Development Bank. The Scopus and Google Scholar databases were preferred over other indexes due to their potential to combat predatory publishing and protect the integrity of the scholarly record. The authors entered the following keywords: TCFD, climate-risk disclosures, and South Africa, using Boolean combinations, for the period from 2015 to the present. The period from 2015 onwards was chosen because 2015 was the year when the TCFD was established by the Financial Stability Board (FSB) to promote climate-related disclosures of financial risks and opportunities, initially focusing on private sector entities. 

The authors identified more than 1000 documents from both databases and other sources related to this review. The initial search yielded 357 articles from the Scopus and Google Scholar databases, while 19 documents were obtained from other sources. The authors examined discrepancies and reached a consensus on the final inclusion. After removing duplicates and final selection, 32 articles met the inclusion criteria in this systematic review after applying the inclusion selection criteria (kindly note Table 1). During the review process, 79 documents were selected based on title screening, while abstract screening obtained a total of 52 documents. 

The main limitation encountered by the authors during the review process was that the Scopus database did not fully address the TCFD as it is implemented in South Africa, but focused more on sustainability reporting and climate disclosures in general. The Google Scholar database and authoritative documents published by other credible organisations mitigated the limitation.

documents.title: Conceptual perspectives on climate risk disclosures for businesses and public sector
documents.snippet:
Climate-related financial disclosures have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their potential to reduce information asymmetries, enable risk-informed investment, and strengthen market and financial system stability (Edwards et al. 2020). Carney (2015) emphasized the need for improved transparency and disclosure of climate risks to allow investors to make more informed decisions. Since then, several climate risk disclosure frameworks have emerged, each with its own focus and strengths. 

The most prominent of these include the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), the Climate Disclosure Standards Board (CDSB), the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), and the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). While the GRI and CDSB emphasize sustainability and environmental performance, and SASB focuses on sector-specific financial materiality, the TCFD distinguishes itself by providing a standardized framework to promote alignment across different jurisdictions and existing regimes (TCFD 2023). The TCFD, established by the Financial Stability Board in 2015, represents a step-change in climate disclosure by targeting how climate risks, both physical and transition, affect financial outcomes and institutional stability. Its recommendations are structured around four key themes: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets (TCFD 2017). This structure supports consistency and comparability across firms and sectors, while encouraging forward-looking scenario analysis. Unlike many earlier frameworks, the TCFD is designed specifically to integrate climate risk into core corporate governance and financial reporting practices. 

The strength of the TCFD framework is enhanced by its increasing global uptake and regulatory integration. Countries such as the UK, New Zealand, and members of the EU have incorporated TCFD principles into mandatory disclosure legislation. Its emphasis on financially material, decision-useful information has made it more appealing to investors and regulators, although this focus on measurable risks may overlook complex or longerterm climate threats that resist easy quantification. The TCFD has also become a foundational model for international harmonization efforts, with the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) explicitly building on its recommendations to establish a global baseline for climate-related financial disclosures (Australian Government, The Treasury 2022).

attempts.answer:
Summary answer
Overall, evidence from Sub‑Saharan Africa indicates that climate risk disclosure can improve financial reporting quality (FRQ) in non‑financial firms, especially where formal enforcement of financial accounting standards is weak, primarily by reducing earnings management and enhancing transparency and accountability; however, effects are heterogeneous across environmental, social, and governance pillars, and outcomes depend on capacity, credibility (e.g., assurance), and alignment with international frameworks such as TCFD and IFRS S1/S2. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">Rising global pressure and adoption of TCFD have increased the comparability and structure of climate-related disclosures, providing a framework that aligns disclosures with investor needs and regulatory expectations</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">Across SSA, weak enforcement and capacity constraints have historically reduced the accuracy of financial reporting, with smaller and non‑listed entities suffering more from errors and inconsistencies</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Across 48 SSA multinational corporations (2010–2019), environmental and social sustainability reporting was associated with significantly lower discretionary accruals (adj. R2=0.33, p<.05), indicating improved earnings quality</cite>, while firm‑level governance quality and economic sustainability disclosures related positively to accruals, underscoring heterogeneity across pillars and governance.

Context: weak enforcement and the role of climate disclosure
SSA financial reporting quality has been constrained by weak enforcement, limited technical capacity, and uneven auditor oversight, so that even when IFRS or local standards are in place, errors and inconsistencies persist, particularly for smaller or non‑listed firms. <cite id="c6678c48-0">In Kenya and Ghana, studies document persistent reporting errors linked to enforcement gaps, inadequate governance, and limited training and oversight</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">In Zambia’s mining sector, IFRS adoption improved reporting quality, but weak regulator capacity and enforcement limited consistent accuracy</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">Similarly, smaller firms in Kenya face difficulties complying with IFRS, leading to errors and inaccuracies despite reforms</cite>. Against this backdrop, climate risk disclosure can act as a complementary or substitute mechanism: investor and financing demands increasingly require climate‑related risk integration and disclosure, pushing firms to improve data quality, governance, and transparency even without strong baseline enforcement.

<cite id="5a5ad33a-2">The TCFD framework provides standardized recommendations for climate‑related financial disclosures that are adaptable across sectors and emphasize investor benefits, while CDP’s investor‑led platform institutionalizes voluntary disclosure and rising response rates</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">Adoption of TCFD among large firms has more than doubled in two years (to ~61% in 2022), reflecting growing alignment to credible global standards</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">IRSF S1 and S2 (2023) codify sustainability and climate‑related disclosures into mainstream reporting, but readiness in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa remains uneven due to limited technical expertise, resource constraints, and weak enforcement; many firms disclose voluntarily with gaps in consistency and comparability</cite>.

Mechanisms linking climate risk disclosure to FRQ under weak enforcement
Two reinforcing mechanisms link climate risk disclosure to higher FRQ in SSA. First, climate disclosure expands the data basis and oversight regime, reducing information asymmetry and disciplining management behavior. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">In SSA multinationals, environmental and social reporting was negatively associated with discretionary accruals, implying lower earnings management and better earnings quality</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-2">The same firms’ sustainability disclosures were assessed for GRI compliance alongside audited financials, enabling a direct link between disclosure scope and accrual‑based manipulation</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-3">Qualitative evidence from Zimbabwe shows that rising regulatory expectations, investor scrutiny, and international financing requirements push firms to integrate climate risks into governance, risk assessments, and annual reporting, improving transparency and visibility even as systems evolve</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-3">Participants noted internal data generation for operational control and strategic planning precedes structured external disclosure, suggesting that climate data pipelines can improve accountability and reduce opportunistic reporting when disclosures are mandated or scrutinized</cite>.

Second, alignment to TCFD/IFRS S1/2 raises the quality bar and creates external comparability, increasing the costs of low‑quality financials. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">A structured review of 134 high‑impact papers finds growing convergence around TCFD and IFRS S2 but persistent regional divergence and concerns that disclosure quality reflects mixed performance and can devolve into symbolic reporting</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-4">In South Africa, integrated reporting and TCFD‑aligned guidance for state‑owned enterprises and the Climate Risk Forum’s minimum disclosure principles embed climate risks into financial reporting processes and governance, supporting improved disclosures and decision‑usefulness</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">By contrast, where enforcement and expertise are weak, voluntary disclosure can suffer from inconsistencies and lower quality, leaving firms with information gaps that audits may or may not catch</cite>.

Empirical evidence on outcomes in SSA
Direct SSA evidence connects sustainability/climate disclosure to FRQ metrics, with the clearest quantitative link via discretionary accruals:
- Earnings management: <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Across 48 SSA countries and 2010–2019, environmental and social disclosures were associated with significantly lower discretionary accruals, and joint effects on discretionary accruals were significant (adj. R2=0.33; p<.05)</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Governance quality and economic sustainability disclosures showed positive links with accruals, while social and environmental disclosures were negative, implying that the E and S pillars can curb opportunistic accruals</cite>. These results suggest that climate (environmental) disclosure is part of a broader transparency regime that improves earnings quality, even though governance and economic disclosures can have mixed or even opposite effects depending on firm context.
- Debt distress and accounting quality: <cite id="c6678c48-0">Audit and reporting quality have been linked to lower probabilities of debt distress reclassification, with stronger reporting quality reducing errors that trigger reclassification</cite>. While this result is not climate‑specific, it indicates that transparency and robust accounting practices (supported by effective disclosure regimes) stabilize debt outcomes; by extension, credible climate risk disclosure can reduce misclassification risk by surfacing material environmental liabilities.
- Internal data to external reporting: <cite id="c6678c48-3">Firms often build internal climate‑risk data for management and operational control before publishing structured external disclosures, pointing to a channel by which climate disclosure requirements nudge investment in data integrity and risk management that spill over into financial statements</cite>.

Country and sector illustrations
- South Africa: <cite id="5a5ad33a-4">As a regional pioneer, South Africa integrates climate disclosures into financial reporting via integrated reporting and TCFD‑aligned sectoral guidance for SOEs, with national working groups publishing minimum climate disclosure principles; these institutional linkages plausibly raise FRQ by embedding climate risks into governance, measurement, and disclosure</cite>.
- Ghana/Nigeria/South Africa readiness for IFRS S1/S2: <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">Despite widespread voluntary sustainability disclosure, readiness for IFRS S1/S2 is limited by capacity and enforcement gaps, with concerns over consistency, comparability, and disclosure quality; the institutionalization of climate reporting under these standards would likely raise FRQ by standardizing materiality assessments and enhancing auditor oversight</cite>.
- Zimbabwean firms: <cite id="c6678c48-3">Rising expectations from regulators and investors led firms to integrate climate risk into governance and risk processes and into annual reporting, improving transparency and external visibility; however, firms cited inconsistent frameworks and expertise gaps, indicating that disclosure systems were still evolving</cite>.
- Energy sector in SSA: <cite id="5c8ecd55-0">Environmental disclosure is framed as critical for “greening” financial reports and enhancing transparency; failure to disclose risks undermines accountability and legitimacy, especially for energy firms with material environmental obligations</cite>.

Limits, heterogeneity, and the enforcement puzzle
The benefits of climate risk disclosure to FRQ are not uniform. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Environmental and social disclosures reduce discretionary accruals, but governance and economic disclosures can relate positively to accruals, so overall FRQ gains depend on the bundle of disclosures and firm governance</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">Standardization remains incomplete and regional practices vary; effectiveness in reflecting underlying performance is mixed, and symbolic or “greenwashing” concerns persist</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">Weak technical capacity and enforcement in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa can limit disclosure quality and credibility, reducing the disciplining effect on accounting choices</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">Even where IFRS is adopted, enforcement gaps and capacity constraints propagate errors and inconsistencies, suggesting that FRQ improvements hinge not only on accounting standards but also on effective institutional enforcement and support</cite>.

What would strengthen the case
To move from suggestive to strong causal conclusions in SSA, more work is needed that directly links climate risk disclosure to narrowly defined FRQ outcomes under weak enforcement, such as: (i) changes in discretionary accruals, K‑means earnings management, and misstatement risk around the adoption of TCFD/CDP/IFRS S1/S2 or country‑level sustainability mandates; (ii) evidence on restatement and audit event dynamics before/after climate disclosure requirements; and (iii) role of assurance and auditor enforcement in converting voluntary climate disclosure into accounting quality gains. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">Recent structured reviews call for deeper work on determinants and financial consequences, with greater integration of TCFD‑aligned and assurance‑focused designs</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">Empirical readiness studies in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa highlight the need to connect disclosure quality to accounting and audit quality outcomes under local enforcement regimes</cite>.

Practical implications for weak‑enforcement SSA settings
- Climate risk disclosure can function as a credible nudge to improve FRQ by: institutionalizing data collection and risk measurement; elevating governance oversight of material environmental risks; and disciplining earnings management through greater transparency. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Empirical results show lower discretionary accruals associated with environmental and social reporting</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-3">Case evidence shows rising external scrutiny and financing requirements push firms to integrate climate risks into annual reporting and governance</cite>.
- To convert disclosure into robust FRQ, regulators and markets should: adopt and enforce TCFD/IFRS S1/S2 adoption timelines; require auditor attestation or assurance of climate‑related financial disclosures; and strengthen enforcement and technical capacity for listed and large non‑listed firms. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">TCFD’s structured categories support comparability and alignment with investor needs</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">However, without capacity and enforcement, voluntary disclosure risks inconsistency and limited impact</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-4">South Africa’s experience shows institutional anchoring of climate disclosures in integrated/financial reporting improves decision relevance</cite>.

Bottom line
In Sub‑Saharan Africa, where formal financial reporting enforcement is often weak, climate risk disclosure improves financial reporting quality by increasing transparency, strengthening governance, and reducing opportunistic earnings management, with the strongest empirical evidence showing lower discretionary accruals associated with environmental and social reporting; nonetheless, gains vary by disclosure pillar and governance quality, and are contingent on capacity and credible assurance and enforcement to prevent symbolic reporting. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Environmental and social climate disclosures are associated with significantly lower discretionary accruals in SSA multinationals</cite>, and <cite id="c6678c48-3">rising investor and regulatory expectations have pushed firms to integrate climate risk into governance and annual reporting, improving transparency</cite>, while <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">weak enforcement and expertise remain the key constraints to turning voluntary climate disclosure into consistently higher accounting quality across SSA</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">Adoption of TCFD frameworks and alignment to IFRS S1/S2 provide credible structures that can enhance comparability and investor alignment</cite>, suggesting targeted policy mixes (mandates with phased compliance, assurance, and capacity building) are most likely to translate climate disclosure into durable FRQ improvements under weak enforcement conditions. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">Regional divergence and greenwashing concerns underscore the need to strengthen disclosure quality and enforcement</cite>.

Title: Managerial Sensemaking of Climate Policy Uncertainty: Environmental Management Accounting and Climate Risk Disclosure in Zimbabwean Firms
Snippet: Participants in the case agreed that although the disclosures have not yet fully aligned with global best practices, organisations in the financial case are mandated to integrate climate-related risks into their broader risk management and annual reporting. In this regard, climate-related risks have been slowly integrated into governance discussions, enterprise assessments, sustainability reporting language, and ESG oversight structures, thereby increasing their visibility and improving the case's image. The participants in this sector pointed out that they have been pushed to do good because of growing regulatory expectations, investor scrutiny, and, above all, international financing requirements that call upon firms to improve quality, consistency, and transparency on issues regarding climate-related disclosures, which have left them with no option but to adhere. Although this trend was consistent with stronger climate risk expectations placed on them by the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, which is the regulator, participants indicated that they were still experiencing some challenges, which included limited technical expertise, inconsistent reporting frameworks, and uncertainty brought by changing regulations, suggesting that the disclosure systems were still evolving and had not yet been institutionalised. 

Participants in the financial services and manufacturing sectors also associated rising disclosure expectations with broader global developments in sustainability reporting, including growing awareness of international climate-related disclosure frameworks and investor expectations for environmental accountability. 

In the quarry mining sector, disclosure was more tentative. One participant had this to say: "Maybe the reason why we have been reactive and not taken a proactive approach to sustainability disclosure is due to the fact that Zimbabwe does not have a standard guideline that has been structured for the Zimbabwean context, and what is prescribed to us are standards developed from stable economies, which, when we try them, do not work here." (P10) 

The food processing sector exhibited a similar trend of partial development in sustainability disclosure. Participants in this sector described disclosure systems that captured environmental metrics and operational trends and emphasised that climate-risk integration was still in its infancy but was developing. 

These narratives from participants suggest that internal data generation may precede external disclosure by a considerable margin: in many firms, environmental and climate risk-related data were already being collected but were not appearing in structured external sustainability disclosures. Participants in this study pointed out that firms utilised internal environmental data for operational control, cost management, and strategic planning, rather than for external disclosure.

Title: Financial reporting quality and the performance of firms in Sub-Sahara Africa: The mediating role of firms’ characteristics
Snippet: In the literature, high-quality financial reports have been linked mostly to larger firms. In fact, the debate in the literature is that accounting numbers denoted in financial statements should be of high quality so as to guarantee investors' confidence and hence the performance of firms. Prior studies by Asyik et al. (2023);Rathnayake et al. (2021) and Sani et al. (2023) suggest that high-quality financial accounting information has the tendency to positively and significantly affect firms' performance; however, whether this is the case for publicly quoted industrial and consumer goods firms in sub-Saharan Africa has been left unresearched. 

A disaggregated financial reporting quality, firm characteristics, and performance model was developed to resolve the lacuna in the accounting literature. First, the results indicated that financial reporting quality positively and insignificantly affects performance (ROA, ROE). On the other hand, firm size was found to significantly mediate the relationship between financial reporting quality and firms' performance. Thus, a statistical factor (firm size) is able to produce quality financial reporting and increase the performance of firms in sub-Saharan Africa. The results in part agree with the findings of Djaballah (2019); Ogbonnaya and Amauwa (2019); Rathnayake et al. 

(2021); Sani et al. (2023) and Asyik et al. (2023) who found that high-quality financial accounting information and firms' performance are linked with the size of the firm. 

The theoretical implication showed that positive theory, which explains choices and methods in financial statement preparation, is reflected in the faithful representation of the components of financial statements. Overall, with firm size introduction in our model, financial reporting quality and firms' pe rformance were positively significantly affected; hence, a statistic factor (firm size) is able to produce quality financial reports and increase the performance of publicly quoted firms in sub-Saharan Africa.

Title: Quality, determinants and financial consequences of climate change disclosures: a structured review
Snippet: this study presents a structured review of empirical research on climate change disclosure, analyzing 134 articles published in journals ranked 2 or higher according to the aBS 2024 journal ranking, spanning from January 2010 to January 2025. Following the implementation of the Paris agreement in 2016 and the release of the tcFD recommendations in 2017, companies have been facing growing pressure to disclose information on climate-related risks and opportunities, driven by global efforts to limit warming. we also noticed a notable rise in related research, especially during the last two years 2023-2024. the review synthesizes findings on different themes related to climate reporting, e.g. the characteristics of climate disclosures, the quality and extent of reporting, determinants of climate reporting, financial implications and issues such as greenwashing allegations and legitimacy concerns. 

this structured review contributes to the existing literature by examining both climate risks/carbon disclosures based on cDP, and climate-related risks and opportunities disclosures guided by the tcFD recommendations. Prior literature research has concentrated on carbon disclosure alone ignoring climate-related disclosures based on tcFD recommendations (e.g. alam & costa, 2025;Borghei, 2021;Shui et al., 2023;wang, 2023). Recognizing the limitations of previous reviews, this review expands the analysis by incorporating climate change disclosures based on both cDP and tcFD recommendations. Furthermore, the scope of this review extends beyond previous studies by adding a broader array of themes. it notably addresses the historical evolution of climate change disclosures, characteristics of climate disclosures, quality of climate reporting and the determinants climate reporting, and explores the critical issue of greenwashing, explicitly linking it to disclosure quality. this thematic integration has not been covered in prior literature reviews. Moreover, this review covers high-impact articles indexed in the aBS journal guide 2024. 

the structured review identified several critical insights regarding climate change disclosures. First, there are efforts toward convergence in climate reporting standards, particularly driven by frameworks, such as the tcFD and iFRS S2; however, global standardization remains incomplete due to differing regional practices and regulatory contexts. additionally, while climate disclosures are increasing, their effectiveness in reflecting actual environmental performance is mixed, raising concerns about symbolic reporting and greenwashing.

Title: Climate risk and financial disclosure in salmon aquaculture
Snippet: Investors' demand for better climate-related financial disclosures has increased (Hahn et al., 2015). The TCFD (2017) suggests that the fear of potential climate-related financial impacts can drive companies to conduct regular climate-related financial disclosures. Task Force's aim is to provide a standardize framework with sufficient information and instructions that will assist financial risk managers in constructing better climate-related financial disclosures. Table 3 presents the major TCFD (2017) recommendations to be followed when creating climate-related financial disclosures. These recommendations are created with the purpose to be easily adaptable across various sectors including the salmon aquaculture industry. They can be seen as suggested steps the financial risk managers of a company should follow when creating climate-related financial disclosures. The recommendations aim to provide a holistic approach for constructing climate-related financial disclosures as well as emphasize the benefits of such disclosures for investors, and other stakeholders. 

Carbon Disclosure project (CDP) 

The Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) was established in 2003 as an investor-led nonprofit initiative, and it began surveying large firms regarding their carbon-related risks and strategies. The main objectives of the CDP are twofold: to inform risk managers about the concerns of investors over climate-related risks and to inform investors about the climate-related risks the firms are exposed to (Stanny & Ely, 2008). To maintain the first objective, the CDP developed a questionnaire by translating the TCFD recommendations into actual disclosure questions and a standardized annual format. The CDP provides investors with a unique platform where the TCFD framework can be brought into real-world practice. The questionnaire is distributed to a range of firms across sectors with high market value. To achieve the second objective, the CDP decided to make the responses of individual firms publicly available online and produce reports with accumulated responses. 

Considering that answering the CDP questionnaire is voluntary, the response rate has been rising gradually. Several studies indicate that an increasing number of firms submit the CDP questionnaire (Lewis et al., 2014;Luo et al., 2012;Stanny & Ely, 2008;Wegener et al., 2013).

Title: Repurposing the use of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework for South Africa’s public sector
Snippet: The MPPI framework aligns with the principles of integrated reporting and emphasizes the need for a holistic, integrated reporting approach that incorporates climate disclosures in the public sector (The Republic of South Africa, 2007). In sub-Saharan Africa, South Africa is widely regarded as a pioneering nation in implementing comprehensive integrated reporting, which began in 2010, with the broad aim of providing investors and other decision-makers with an all-inclusive view of an organisation's performance based on environmental, social, and governance factors (ESG) (ACCA, 2015). For instance, companies that are majority state-owned and listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange are required to integrate climate disclosures into their financial reporting, which includes Telkom SOC Ltd and Transnet SOC Ltd, among others. 

Furthermore, the South African government, through its National Treasury, established the Climate Risk Forum and Disclosure Working Group in 2021 to guide private and sector organisations to report on climate-related financial risks and opportunities. For example, in December 2021, the Climate Risk Forum and Disclosure Working Group, with financial and technical support from the World Bank's International Finance Corporation and other stakeholders, produced the Principles and Guidance for Minimum Disclosure of Climate-Related Risks and Opportunities based on the TCFD recommendations to influence sustainability reporting in the public sector (The Climate Risk Forum, 2021). While central and local governments, as well as SOEs in South Africa, are at different levels of implementation of sustainability reporting, adapting the TCFD recommendations could provide these public sector entities with a holistic and comprehensive assessment of climate-related financial risks and opportunities emanating from their operations (Ding et al., 2023). The implementation of the TCFD framework in South Africa's public sector can support central and local government organisations and SOEs to improve climate-related financial disclosures, understand stakeholder needs, and review their climate-related opportunities and risks (O'Dwyer & Unerman, 2020). Furthermore, adopting TCFD recommendations supports public sector organisations in mainstreaming climate change issues in their operations. It enables them to be proactive and obtain useful decision-making information that supports management, investments, and sustainable development (Di Marco et al., 2023).

Overall, evidence from Sub‑Saharan Africa indicates that climate risk disclosure can improve financial reporting quality (FRQ) in non‑financial firms, especially where formal enforcement of financial accounting standards is weak, primarily by reducing earnings management and enhancing transparency and accountability; however, effects are heterogeneous across environmental, social, and governance pillars, and outcomes depend on capacity, credibility (e.g., assurance), and alignment with international frameworks such as TCFD and IFRS S1/S2. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">Rising global pressure and adoption of TCFD have increased the comparability and structure of climate-related disclosures, providing a framework that aligns disclosures with investor needs and regulatory expectations</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">Across SSA, weak enforcement and capacity constraints have historically reduced the accuracy of financial reporting, with smaller and non‑listed entities suffering more from errors and inconsistencies</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Across 48 SSA multinational corporations (2010–2019), environmental and social sustainability reporting was associated with significantly lower discretionary accruals (adj. R2=0.33, p<.05), indicating improved earnings quality</cite>, while firm‑level governance quality and economic sustainability disclosures related positively to accruals, underscoring heterogeneity across pillars and governance.

Context: weak enforcement and the role of climate disclosure
SSA financial reporting quality has been constrained by weak enforcement, limited technical capacity, and uneven auditor oversight, so that even when IFRS or local standards are in place, errors and inconsistencies persist, particularly for smaller or non‑listed firms. <cite id="c6678c48-0">In Kenya and Ghana, studies document persistent reporting errors linked to enforcement gaps, inadequate governance, and limited training and oversight</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">In Zambia’s mining sector, IFRS adoption improved reporting quality, but weak regulator capacity and enforcement limited consistent accuracy</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">Similarly, smaller firms in Kenya face difficulties complying with IFRS, leading to errors and inaccuracies despite reforms</cite>. Against this backdrop, climate risk disclosure can act as a complementary or substitute mechanism: investor and financing demands increasingly require climate‑related risk integration and disclosure, pushing firms to improve data quality, governance, and transparency even without strong baseline enforcement.

<cite id="5a5ad33a-2">The TCFD framework provides standardized recommendations for climate‑related financial disclosures that are adaptable across sectors and emphasize investor benefits, while CDP’s investor‑led platform institutionalizes voluntary disclosure and rising response rates</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">Adoption of TCFD among large firms has more than doubled in two years (to ~61% in 2022), reflecting growing alignment to credible global standards</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">IRSF S1 and S2 (2023) codify sustainability and climate‑related disclosures into mainstream reporting, but readiness in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa remains uneven due to limited technical expertise, resource constraints, and weak enforcement; many firms disclose voluntarily with gaps in consistency and comparability</cite>.

Mechanisms linking climate risk disclosure to FRQ under weak enforcement
Two reinforcing mechanisms link climate risk disclosure to higher FRQ in SSA. First, climate disclosure expands the data basis and oversight regime, reducing information asymmetry and disciplining management behavior. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">In SSA multinationals, environmental and social reporting was negatively associated with discretionary accruals, implying lower earnings management and better earnings quality</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-2">The same firms’ sustainability disclosures were assessed for GRI compliance alongside audited financials, enabling a direct link between disclosure scope and accrual‑based manipulation</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-3">Qualitative evidence from Zimbabwe shows that rising regulatory expectations, investor scrutiny, and international financing requirements push firms to integrate climate risks into governance, risk assessments, and annual reporting, improving transparency and visibility even as systems evolve</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-3">Participants noted internal data generation for operational control and strategic planning precedes structured external disclosure, suggesting that climate data pipelines can improve accountability and reduce opportunistic reporting when disclosures are mandated or scrutinized</cite>.

Second, alignment to TCFD/IFRS S1/2 raises the quality bar and creates external comparability, increasing the costs of low‑quality financials. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">A structured review of 134 high‑impact papers finds growing convergence around TCFD and IFRS S2 but persistent regional divergence and concerns that disclosure quality reflects mixed performance and can devolve into symbolic reporting</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-4">In South Africa, integrated reporting and TCFD‑aligned guidance for state‑owned enterprises and the Climate Risk Forum’s minimum disclosure principles embed climate risks into financial reporting processes and governance, supporting improved disclosures and decision‑usefulness</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">By contrast, where enforcement and expertise are weak, voluntary disclosure can suffer from inconsistencies and lower quality, leaving firms with information gaps that audits may or may not catch</cite>.

Empirical evidence on outcomes in SSA
Direct SSA evidence connects sustainability/climate disclosure to FRQ metrics, with the clearest quantitative link via discretionary accruals:
- Earnings management: <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Across 48 SSA countries and 2010–2019, environmental and social disclosures were associated with significantly lower discretionary accruals, and joint effects on discretionary accruals were significant (adj. R2=0.33; p<.05)</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Governance quality and economic sustainability disclosures showed positive links with accruals, while social and environmental disclosures were negative, implying that the E and S pillars can curb opportunistic accruals</cite>. These results suggest that climate (environmental) disclosure is part of a broader transparency regime that improves earnings quality, even though governance and economic disclosures can have mixed or even opposite effects depending on firm context.
- Debt distress and accounting quality: <cite id="c6678c48-0">Audit and reporting quality have been linked to lower probabilities of debt distress reclassification, with stronger reporting quality reducing errors that trigger reclassification</cite>. While this result is not climate‑specific, it indicates that transparency and robust accounting practices (supported by effective disclosure regimes) stabilize debt outcomes; by extension, credible climate risk disclosure can reduce misclassification risk by surfacing material environmental liabilities.
- Internal data to external reporting: <cite id="c6678c48-3">Firms often build internal climate‑risk data for management and operational control before publishing structured external disclosures, pointing to a channel by which climate disclosure requirements nudge investment in data integrity and risk management that spill over into financial statements</cite>.

Country and sector illustrations
- South Africa: <cite id="5a5ad33a-4">As a regional pioneer, South Africa integrates climate disclosures into financial reporting via integrated reporting and TCFD‑aligned sectoral guidance for SOEs, with national working groups publishing minimum climate disclosure principles; these institutional linkages plausibly raise FRQ by embedding climate risks into governance, measurement, and disclosure</cite>.
- Ghana/Nigeria/South Africa readiness for IFRS S1/S2: <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">Despite widespread voluntary sustainability disclosure, readiness for IFRS S1/S2 is limited by capacity and enforcement gaps, with concerns over consistency, comparability, and disclosure quality; the institutionalization of climate reporting under these standards would likely raise FRQ by standardizing materiality assessments and enhancing auditor oversight</cite>.
- Zimbabwean firms: <cite id="c6678c48-3">Rising expectations from regulators and investors led firms to integrate climate risk into governance and risk processes and into annual reporting, improving transparency and external visibility; however, firms cited inconsistent frameworks and expertise gaps, indicating that disclosure systems were still evolving</cite>.
- Energy sector in SSA: <cite id="5c8ecd55-0">Environmental disclosure is framed as critical for “greening” financial reports and enhancing transparency; failure to disclose risks undermines accountability and legitimacy, especially for energy firms with material environmental obligations</cite>.

Limits, heterogeneity, and the enforcement puzzle
The benefits of climate risk disclosure to FRQ are not uniform. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Environmental and social disclosures reduce discretionary accruals, but governance and economic disclosures can relate positively to accruals, so overall FRQ gains depend on the bundle of disclosures and firm governance</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">Standardization remains incomplete and regional practices vary; effectiveness in reflecting underlying performance is mixed, and symbolic or “greenwashing” concerns persist</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">Weak technical capacity and enforcement in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa can limit disclosure quality and credibility, reducing the disciplining effect on accounting choices</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-0">Even where IFRS is adopted, enforcement gaps and capacity constraints propagate errors and inconsistencies, suggesting that FRQ improvements hinge not only on accounting standards but also on effective institutional enforcement and support</cite>.

What would strengthen the case
To move from suggestive to strong causal conclusions in SSA, more work is needed that directly links climate risk disclosure to narrowly defined FRQ outcomes under weak enforcement, such as: (i) changes in discretionary accruals, K‑means earnings management, and misstatement risk around the adoption of TCFD/CDP/IFRS S1/S2 or country‑level sustainability mandates; (ii) evidence on restatement and audit event dynamics before/after climate disclosure requirements; and (iii) role of assurance and auditor enforcement in converting voluntary climate disclosure into accounting quality gains. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">Recent structured reviews call for deeper work on determinants and financial consequences, with greater integration of TCFD‑aligned and assurance‑focused designs</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">Empirical readiness studies in Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa highlight the need to connect disclosure quality to accounting and audit quality outcomes under local enforcement regimes</cite>.

Practical implications for weak‑enforcement SSA settings
- Climate risk disclosure can function as a credible nudge to improve FRQ by: institutionalizing data collection and risk measurement; elevating governance oversight of material environmental risks; and disciplining earnings management through greater transparency. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Empirical results show lower discretionary accruals associated with environmental and social reporting</cite>. <cite id="c6678c48-3">Case evidence shows rising external scrutiny and financing requirements push firms to integrate climate risks into annual reporting and governance</cite>.
- To convert disclosure into robust FRQ, regulators and markets should: adopt and enforce TCFD/IFRS S1/S2 adoption timelines; require auditor attestation or assurance of climate‑related financial disclosures; and strengthen enforcement and technical capacity for listed and large non‑listed firms. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">TCFD’s structured categories support comparability and alignment with investor needs</cite>. <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">However, without capacity and enforcement, voluntary disclosure risks inconsistency and limited impact</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-4">South Africa’s experience shows institutional anchoring of climate disclosures in integrated/financial reporting improves decision relevance</cite>.

Bottom line
In Sub‑Saharan Africa, where formal financial reporting enforcement is often weak, climate risk disclosure improves financial reporting quality by increasing transparency, strengthening governance, and reducing opportunistic earnings management, with the strongest empirical evidence showing lower discretionary accruals associated with environmental and social reporting; nonetheless, gains vary by disclosure pillar and governance quality, and are contingent on capacity and credible assurance and enforcement to prevent symbolic reporting. <cite id="5c8ecd55-3">Environmental and social climate disclosures are associated with significantly lower discretionary accruals in SSA multinationals</cite>, and <cite id="c6678c48-3">rising investor and regulatory expectations have pushed firms to integrate climate risk into governance and annual reporting, improving transparency</cite>, while <cite id="5c8ecd55-1">weak enforcement and expertise remain the key constraints to turning voluntary climate disclosure into consistently higher accounting quality across SSA</cite>. <cite id="5a5ad33a-0">Adoption of TCFD frameworks and alignment to IFRS S1/S2 provide credible structures that can enhance comparability and investor alignment</cite>, suggesting targeted policy mixes (mandates with phased compliance, assurance, and capacity building) are most likely to translate climate disclosure into durable FRQ improvements under weak enforcement conditions. <cite id="5a5ad33a-1">Regional divergence and greenwashing concerns underscore the need to strengthen disclosure quality and enforcement</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Influence of Accounting Information Systems (AIS) on Financial Reporting Accuracy
Snippet: In Kenya, another Sub-Saharan African country, there have been efforts to enhance financial reporting accuracy through the adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) Bonface Kimani ( 2024) and the establishment of regulatory bodies like the Capital Markets Authority (CMA). However, a study by Ochieng, et al. (2018) found that smaller companies and non-listed entities often face difficulties in complying with these standards, leading to reporting errors and inaccuracies. 

In Sub-Saharan Africa, the challenges related to financial reporting accuracy are compounded by factors like political instability, inadequate infrastructure, and limited access to technology. Addressing these challenges requires sustained efforts in capacity building, regulatory enforcement, and the promotion of transparent reporting practices. 

In Sub-Saharan African economies, the issue of financial reporting accuracy remains a complex challenge. In Ghana, for example, a study by Sackey, et al. (2017) examined the quality of financial reporting in the banking sector and identified various factors affecting reporting accuracy. These factors included inadequate corporate governance practices, insufficiently trained staff, and a lack of regulatory oversight. Despite efforts by the Bank of Ghana to strengthen reporting standards, the country continues to grapple with reporting errors in the financial sector. 

In Zambia, a study by Mooya (2014) investigated the quality of financial reporting in the mining sector, a vital industry in the country. The research found that while there were improvements in reporting quality following the adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), challenges such as weak enforcement and limited capacity among regulatory bodies hindered consistent reporting accuracy. 

Overall, Sub-Saharan African economies face systemic challenges in achieving financial reporting accuracy, ranging from governance and regulatory issues to capacity limitations. Addressing these challenges necessitates a multi-pronged approach that includes improving corporate governance practices, enhancing regulatory oversight, providing training and technical assistance, and promoting transparency and accountability in financial reporting. 

Accounting Information Systems (AIS) sophistication, as measured by the level of automation and integration, plays a critical role in influencing financial reporting accuracy. One level of sophistication involves manual or decentralized systems, where data is processed and recorded manually without the aid of integrated software.

Title: Firm-specific characteristics and environmental disclosure of energy firms in Sub-Saharan Africa
Snippet: Amidst the vast and diverse landscapes of sub-Saharan Africa, the energy sector has emerged as a powerful catalyst driving economic progress and development, energizing industries, homes, and communities alike. However, this relentless growth in energy demand, propelled by a burgeoning population and expanding economies, comes hand in hand with an equally pressing challenge: environmental sustainability. 

In 2021, environmental sustainability took center stage as over 40,000 people, including 120 world leaders, 22,274 party delegates, 14,124 observers, and 3,886 media representatives, gathered in Glasgow, Scotland for the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP26). The event spanned two weeks and captivated global attention, with evidence, solutions, political will to act, and concrete signals of climate change action at the forefront of discussions (UN, 2021). Environmental disclosure has emerged as a crucial instrument at this critical juncture to address climate change and its consequences, offering valuable insights into corporate responsibility and transparency. 

Environmental disclosure can be considered critical for fostering stakeholder engagement and driving the "greening" of corporate financial reports. Tukur, Shehu, Mammadi, and Sulaiman (2019) stated that a firm can carry out corporate social responsibility by involving environmental conservation and sustainability activities. According to Nweze and Nwadialor (2020), environmental disclosure entails disclosing expenses incurred by a company to preserve and enhance its local environment in its annual report. In doing so, firms become more transparent about their investments in environmental protection, particularly when these expenditures are linked to operations that negatively impact the natural world. 

In light of this, Jeroh (2020) highlights the significance of listed firms in sub-Saharan Africa, especially those in the energy industry, reporting their environmental obligations to the public. Failure to do so may hinder transparency, accountability, and the acquisition of legitimacy and recognition from stakeholders. This has prompted numerous studies underlining the need for better environmental performance, disclosure standards, and further recommendations for businesses to adopt eco-friendly practices. Environmental disclosure has emerged as a central discourse in accounting literature because of the mounting pressure to fulfill many environmental obligations across various industries. 

Regrettably, despite the increasing emphasis on environmental sustainability, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the factors influencing environmental disclosure practices among sub-Saharan African energy firms.

Title: Managerial Sensemaking of Climate Policy Uncertainty: Environmental Management Accounting and Climate Risk Disclosure in Zimbabwean Firms
Snippet: Participants in the case agreed that although the disclosures have not yet fully aligned with global best practices, organisations in the financial case are mandated to integrate climate-related risks into their broader risk management and annual reporting. In this regard, climate-related risks have been slowly integrated into governance discussions, enterprise assessments, sustainability reporting language, and ESG oversight structures, thereby increasing their visibility and improving the case's image. The participants in this sector pointed out that they have been pushed to do good because of growing regulatory expectations, investor scrutiny, and, above all, international financing requirements that call upon firms to improve quality, consistency, and transparency on issues regarding climate-related disclosures, which have left them with no option but to adhere. Although this trend was consistent with stronger climate risk expectations placed on them by the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, which is the regulator, participants indicated that they were still experiencing some challenges, which included limited technical expertise, inconsistent reporting frameworks, and uncertainty brought by changing regulations, suggesting that the disclosure systems were still evolving and had not yet been institutionalised. 

Participants in the financial services and manufacturing sectors also associated rising disclosure expectations with broader global developments in sustainability reporting, including growing awareness of international climate-related disclosure frameworks and investor expectations for environmental accountability. 

In the quarry mining sector, disclosure was more tentative. One participant had this to say: "Maybe the reason why we have been reactive and not taken a proactive approach to sustainability disclosure is due to the fact that Zimbabwe does not have a standard guideline that has been structured for the Zimbabwean context, and what is prescribed to us are standards developed from stable economies, which, when we try them, do not work here." (P10) 

The food processing sector exhibited a similar trend of partial development in sustainability disclosure. Participants in this sector described disclosure systems that captured environmental metrics and operational trends and emphasised that climate-risk integration was still in its infancy but was developing. 

These narratives from participants suggest that internal data generation may precede external disclosure by a considerable margin: in many firms, environmental and climate risk-related data were already being collected but were not appearing in structured external sustainability disclosures. Participants in this study pointed out that firms utilised internal environmental data for operational control, cost management, and strategic planning, rather than for external disclosure.

Title: Financial reporting quality and the performance of firms in Sub-Sahara Africa: The mediating role of firms’ characteristics
Snippet: In the literature, high-quality financial reports have been linked mostly to larger firms. In fact, the debate in the literature is that accounting numbers denoted in financial statements should be of high quality so as to guarantee investors' confidence and hence the performance of firms. Prior studies by Asyik et al. (2023);Rathnayake et al. (2021) and Sani et al. (2023) suggest that high-quality financial accounting information has the tendency to positively and significantly affect firms' performance; however, whether this is the case for publicly quoted industrial and consumer goods firms in sub-Saharan Africa has been left unresearched. 

A disaggregated financial reporting quality, firm characteristics, and performance model was developed to resolve the lacuna in the accounting literature. First, the results indicated that financial reporting quality positively and insignificantly affects performance (ROA, ROE). On the other hand, firm size was found to significantly mediate the relationship between financial reporting quality and firms' performance. Thus, a statistical factor (firm size) is able to produce quality financial reporting and increase the performance of firms in sub-Saharan Africa. The results in part agree with the findings of Djaballah (2019); Ogbonnaya and Amauwa (2019); Rathnayake et al. 

(2021); Sani et al. (2023) and Asyik et al. (2023) who found that high-quality financial accounting information and firms' performance are linked with the size of the firm. 

The theoretical implication showed that positive theory, which explains choices and methods in financial statement preparation, is reflected in the faithful representation of the components of financial statements. Overall, with firm size introduction in our model, financial reporting quality and firms' pe rformance were positively significantly affected; hence, a statistic factor (firm size) is able to produce quality financial reports and increase the performance of publicly quoted firms in sub-Saharan Africa.

documents.title: Financial reporting quality and the performance of firms in Sub-Sahara Africa: The mediating role of firms’ characteristics
documents.snippet:
In the literature, high-quality financial reports have been linked mostly to larger firms. In fact, the debate in the literature is that accounting numbers denoted in financial statements should be of high quality so as to guarantee investors' confidence and hence the performance of firms. Prior studies by Asyik et al. (2023);Rathnayake et al. (2021) and Sani et al. (2023) suggest that high-quality financial accounting information has the tendency to positively and significantly affect firms' performance; however, whether this is the case for publicly quoted industrial and consumer goods firms in sub-Saharan Africa has been left unresearched. 

A disaggregated financial reporting quality, firm characteristics, and performance model was developed to resolve the lacuna in the accounting literature. First, the results indicated that financial reporting quality positively and insignificantly affects performance (ROA, ROE). On the other hand, firm size was found to significantly mediate the relationship between financial reporting quality and firms' performance. Thus, a statistical factor (firm size) is able to produce quality financial reporting and increase the performance of firms in sub-Saharan Africa. The results in part agree with the findings of Djaballah (2019); Ogbonnaya and Amauwa (2019); Rathnayake et al. 

(2021); Sani et al. (2023) and Asyik et al. (2023) who found that high-quality financial accounting information and firms' performance are linked with the size of the firm. 

The theoretical implication showed that positive theory, which explains choices and methods in financial statement preparation, is reflected in the faithful representation of the components of financial statements. Overall, with firm size introduction in our model, financial reporting quality and firms' pe rformance were positively significantly affected; hence, a statistic factor (firm size) is able to produce quality financial reports and increase the performance of publicly quoted firms in sub-Saharan Africa.

Title: Quality, determinants and financial consequences of climate change disclosures: a structured review
Snippet: the regulatory pressure has been translated into the establishment of carbon Disclosure Project (cDP) in 2000 to promote the disclosure of climate-related (cDP, 2022). later on, the Financial Stability Board (FSB) established the task Force on climate-related Financial Disclosures (tcFD) in 2017 to provide more consistent guidance on disclosing climate-related financial risks and opportunities (tcFD, 2017). the tcFD recommendations assist firms on how to disclose climate-related information effectively to investors and other stakeholders, categorizing the information into four key areas 'governance, Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics and targets' , these categories are designed to provide a framework that ensures not only the comparability of climate-related disclosures but also supports companies in aligning their reporting with investor and stakeholders needs and regulatory expectations (tcFD, 2017). the kPMg Survey of Sustainability Reporting 2022 shows that adoption of the tcFD recommendations has nearly doubled among the largest global companies across 31 countries in the last 2 years, increasing from 37% in 2021 to 61% at 2022 (kPMg, 2022). given the growing reliance on tcFD, this review highlights emerging topics in climate disclosure and draws on both cDP and tcFD frameworks to provide a more nuanced understanding of the literature in this area. 

Prior reviews have tended to focus on specific strands of the carbon/climate-risk disclosure literature, such as financial consequences, determinants and assurance, while repeatedly calling for deeper work on the drivers of reporting. For instance, Borghei (2021) offers a carbon disclosure systematic review covering a timing frame from 1981 to 2020 centered on the evolution of carbon disclosure, assurance, determinants and quality. He et al. (2022) focused on positioning carbon accounting as a discipline with bring up themes, such as determinants, assurance, carbon management and carbon performance, while wang (2023) focuses primarily on financial consequences of carbon disclosures based on cDP. in addition, ngo et al. ( 2023) contributed to the field by conducting a conceptual analysis and proposing a future research agenda, with a particular focus on studies aligned with the tcFD recommendations and sustainability reporting initiatives.

Title: Quality, determinants and financial consequences of climate change disclosures: a structured review
Snippet: this study presents a structured review of empirical research on climate change disclosure, analyzing 134 articles published in journals ranked 2 or higher according to the aBS 2024 journal ranking, spanning from January 2010 to January 2025. Following the implementation of the Paris agreement in 2016 and the release of the tcFD recommendations in 2017, companies have been facing growing pressure to disclose information on climate-related risks and opportunities, driven by global efforts to limit warming. we also noticed a notable rise in related research, especially during the last two years 2023-2024. the review synthesizes findings on different themes related to climate reporting, e.g. the characteristics of climate disclosures, the quality and extent of reporting, determinants of climate reporting, financial implications and issues such as greenwashing allegations and legitimacy concerns. 

this structured review contributes to the existing literature by examining both climate risks/carbon disclosures based on cDP, and climate-related risks and opportunities disclosures guided by the tcFD recommendations. Prior literature research has concentrated on carbon disclosure alone ignoring climate-related disclosures based on tcFD recommendations (e.g. alam & costa, 2025;Borghei, 2021;Shui et al., 2023;wang, 2023). Recognizing the limitations of previous reviews, this review expands the analysis by incorporating climate change disclosures based on both cDP and tcFD recommendations. Furthermore, the scope of this review extends beyond previous studies by adding a broader array of themes. it notably addresses the historical evolution of climate change disclosures, characteristics of climate disclosures, quality of climate reporting and the determinants climate reporting, and explores the critical issue of greenwashing, explicitly linking it to disclosure quality. this thematic integration has not been covered in prior literature reviews. Moreover, this review covers high-impact articles indexed in the aBS journal guide 2024. 

the structured review identified several critical insights regarding climate change disclosures. First, there are efforts toward convergence in climate reporting standards, particularly driven by frameworks, such as the tcFD and iFRS S2; however, global standardization remains incomplete due to differing regional practices and regulatory contexts. additionally, while climate disclosures are increasing, their effectiveness in reflecting actual environmental performance is mixed, raising concerns about symbolic reporting and greenwashing.

Title: Climate risk and financial disclosure in salmon aquaculture
Snippet: Investors' demand for better climate-related financial disclosures has increased (Hahn et al., 2015). The number of firms across sectors that are pursuing financial disclosures upon investors' requests is on the rise (Reid & Toffel, 2009). The TCFD (2017) suggests that the fear of potential climate-related financial impacts can drive companies to conduct regular climate-related financial disclosures. Task Force's aim is to provide a standardize framework with sufficient information and instructions that will assist financial risk managers in constructing better climate-related financial disclosures. Table 3 presents the major TCFD (2017) recommendations to be followed when creating climate-related financial disclosures. These recommendations are created with the purpose to be easily adaptable across various sectors including the salmon aquaculture industry. They can be seen as suggested steps the financial risk managers of a company should follow when creating climate-related financial disclosures. The recommendations aim to provide a holistic approach for constructing climate-related financial disclosures as well as emphasize the benefits of such disclosures for investors, and other stakeholders. 

Carbon Disclosure project (CDP) 

The Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) was established in 2003 as an investor-led nonprofit initiative, and it began surveying large firms regarding their carbon-related risks and strategies. The main objectives of the CDP are twofold: to inform risk managers about the concerns of investors over climate-related risks and to inform investors about the climate-related risks the firms are exposed to (Stanny & Ely, 2008). To maintain the first objective, the CDP developed a questionnaire by translating the TCFD recommendations into actual disclosure questions and a standardized annual format. The CDP provides investors with a unique platform where the TCFD framework can be brought into real-world practice. The questionnaire is distributed to a range of firms across sectors with high market value. To achieve the second objective, the CDP decided to make the responses of individual firms publicly available online and produce reports with accumulated responses. 

Considering that answering the CDP questionnaire is voluntary, the response rate has been rising gradually. Several studies indicate that an increasing number of firms submit the CDP questionnaire (Lewis et al., 2014;Luo et al., 2012;Stanny & Ely, 2008;Wegener et al., 2013).

Title: KUALITAS PENGUNGKAPAN PELAPORAN IKLIM DENGAN REKOMENDASI TCFD PERUSAHAAN METAL-MINING DAN BANKS TAHUN 2020-2022
Snippet: Climate change has become a concern for every sector, including finance. This is the basis for the creation of the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations. This research aims to determine the quality of climate reporting disclosure following TCFD recommendations. The theories employed in this study are stakeholder theory and legitimacy theory. The content analysis method is utilized to understand and assess the quality of climate reporting disclosure from 18 companies during the period 2020-2022. The results indicate that the majority of companies achieve a moderate quality, suggesting that the implementation of TCFD recommendations is still considered sufficient. The main category of governance and the sub-category of target usage receive the highest rankings, indicating that the disclosure in these categories and sub-categories aligns with TCFD recommendations. The banking sector attains high quality, even though its impact on climate change is not direct. South Africa obtains a high percentage, while the United Kingdom consistently experiences improvement each year.

Title: Repurposing the use of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework for South Africa’s public sector
Snippet: The MPPI framework aligns with the principles of integrated reporting and emphasizes the need for a holistic, integrated reporting approach that incorporates climate disclosures in the public sector (The Republic of South Africa, 2007). In sub-Saharan Africa, South Africa is widely regarded as a pioneering nation in implementing comprehensive integrated reporting, which began in 2010, with the broad aim of providing investors and other decision-makers with an all-inclusive view of an organisation's performance based on environmental, social, and governance factors (ESG) (ACCA, 2015). For instance, companies that are majority state-owned and listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange are required to integrate climate disclosures into their financial reporting, which includes Telkom SOC Ltd and Transnet SOC Ltd, among others. 

Furthermore, the South African government, through its National Treasury, established the Climate Risk Forum and Disclosure Working Group in 2021 to guide private and sector organisations to report on climate-related financial risks and opportunities. For example, in December 2021, the Climate Risk Forum and Disclosure Working Group, with financial and technical support from the World Bank's International Finance Corporation and other stakeholders, produced the Principles and Guidance for Minimum Disclosure of Climate-Related Risks and Opportunities based on the TCFD recommendations to influence sustainability reporting in the public sector (The Climate Risk Forum, 2021). While central and local governments, as well as SOEs in South Africa, are at different levels of implementation of sustainability reporting, adapting the TCFD recommendations could provide these public sector entities with a holistic and comprehensive assessment of climate-related financial risks and opportunities emanating from their operations (Ding et al., 2023). The implementation of the TCFD framework in South Africa's public sector can support central and local government organisations and SOEs to improve climate-related financial disclosures, understand stakeholder needs, and review their climate-related opportunities and risks (O'Dwyer & Unerman, 2020). Furthermore, adopting TCFD recommendations supports public sector organisations in mainstreaming climate change issues in their operations. It enables them to be proactive and obtain useful decision-making information that supports management, investments, and sustainable development (Di Marco et al., 2023).
