Title: Corporate responsibility or corporate illusion? An integrative review analysis of the Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) shortcomings and greenwashing in Sub-Saharan Africa
Snippet: This study examines how environmental, social, and governance malpractices manifest as selective disclosure and weak assurance, enabling greenwashing across corporations in sub–Saharan Africa, and delineates governance and policy levers to curb these behaviors. Following integrative review standards, the study screens Scopus and Web of Science outputs and synthesizes 22 peer-reviewed studies published between 2014 and 2024 using a transparent PRISMA-informed pipeline and thematic coding to ensure replicability and analytic depth. The evidence shows that greenwashing is driven by regulatory gaps, voluntary compliance regimes, and narrative heavy self-reporting, while quality of integrated reporting is unevenly translated into real performance, signalling persistent decoupling between disclosure and outcomes; the preponderance of studies identifies governance weaknesses and selective disclosures as recurrent enablers across sectors including certification schemes and the built environment, corroborating the dominance of symbolic over substantive implementation in many African settings. The review argues for stronger ESG legislation, independent third-party auditing, and digital monitoring tools to restore investor confidence, protect public trust, and align corporate behaviour with the Sustainable Development Goals in sub-Saharan Africa

Title: Evidence of the impact of corporate governance on ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa: the moderating role of ownership structure
Snippet: Despite a significant cultural and socioeconomic difference, little is understood about the interaction of cultural and social contexts with reporting, beyond the images of extreme poverty repeatedly documented in the media (Waweru 2020). However, there is a paucity of studies on the impact of corporate governance on ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). To the best of our knowledge, the only available studies are Waweru (2020), which analyses the disclosure of business ethics and corporate governance in sub-Saharan Africa, together with Githaiga and Kosgei (2023), that examined the board characteristics and sustainability reporting of selected firms from countries in East Africa. Nonetheless, ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa has gained traction as companies recognise the need to address ESG concerns, with the aim of creating value, building trust and contributing to solving significant challenges (Tilt et al. 2021). 

In terms of companies in sub-Saharan Africa, enhanced ESG disclosure practices are crucial to access funding sources and attract investors (Siueia et al. 2019). Improved corporate disclosure practices, including non-financial disclosures, are becoming increasingly influential as stakeholders demand transparency and accountability (e.g. Amran & Keat Ooi 2014;Maas & Sampers 2020). However, recent studies focusing on sub-Saharan Africa have not yet confirmed this evidence. Notably, Githaiga and Kosgei (2023), examined the correlation between the board characteristics and sustainability reporting of listed firms in East Africa. The findings they obtained underlined that board gender diversity, board financial expertise and board independence are positively and significantly associated with sustainability reporting, whereas board size has a negative and significant effect on sustainability reporting. Similarly, Ofoegbu et al. (2018) examined corporate board characteristics and environmental disclosure quantity based on South Africa (integrated reporting) and Nigeria (traditional reporting). The authors determined a significant positive relationship between board independence and environmental disclosure in Nigeria. The research they conducted focused on individual nations or a specific economic bloc. Given that the sub-Saharan region comprises the largest part of the continent, the understanding derived from these particular studies has substantial implications not only for the entire region of Africa, but also for other emerging economies that share similar developmental characteristics.

Title: Firm-specific characteristics and environmental disclosure of energy firms in Sub-Saharan Africa
Snippet: Amidst the vast and diverse landscapes of sub-Saharan Africa, the energy sector has emerged as a powerful catalyst driving economic progress and development, energizing industries, homes, and communities alike. However, this relentless growth in energy demand, propelled by a burgeoning population and expanding economies, comes hand in hand with an equally pressing challenge: environmental sustainability. 

In 2021, environmental sustainability took center stage as over 40,000 people, including 120 world leaders, 22,274 party delegates, 14,124 observers, and 3,886 media representatives, gathered in Glasgow, Scotland for the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP26). The event spanned two weeks and captivated global attention, with evidence, solutions, political will to act, and concrete signals of climate change action at the forefront of discussions (UN, 2021). Environmental disclosure has emerged as a crucial instrument at this critical juncture to address climate change and its consequences, offering valuable insights into corporate responsibility and transparency. 

Environmental disclosure can be considered critical for fostering stakeholder engagement and driving the "greening" of corporate financial reports. Tukur, Shehu, Mammadi, and Sulaiman (2019) stated that a firm can carry out corporate social responsibility by involving environmental conservation and sustainability activities. According to Nweze and Nwadialor (2020), environmental disclosure entails disclosing expenses incurred by a company to preserve and enhance its local environment in its annual report. In doing so, firms become more transparent about their investments in environmental protection, particularly when these expenditures are linked to operations that negatively impact the natural world. 

In light of this, Jeroh (2020) highlights the significance of listed firms in sub-Saharan Africa, especially those in the energy industry, reporting their environmental obligations to the public. Failure to do so may hinder transparency, accountability, and the acquisition of legitimacy and recognition from stakeholders. This has prompted numerous studies underlining the need for better environmental performance, disclosure standards, and further recommendations for businesses to adopt eco-friendly practices. Environmental disclosure has emerged as a central discourse in accounting literature because of the mounting pressure to fulfill many environmental obligations across various industries. 

Regrettably, despite the increasing emphasis on environmental sustainability, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the factors influencing environmental disclosure practices among sub-Saharan African energy firms.

Title: Corporate responsibility or corporate illusion? An integrative review analysis of the Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) shortcomings and greenwashing in Sub-Saharan Africa
Snippet: According to Lashitew (2021), the rapid diffusion of sustainability rhetoric across African markets has outpaced the development and enforcement of credible governance, creating fertile conditions for environmental, social, and governance malpractices that erode trust and misallocate capital. The persistent gap between disclosure and performance has been documented in South Africa's building sector, cotton certification in multiple African countries, and investment markets in Zimbabwe, where selective reporting and weak assurance enable symbolic rather than substantive change to dominate corporate communication ecosystems (Schoeman & Gunter, 2018;Partzsch et al., 2019;Olatubosun & Nyazenga, 2021). This study argues that the central problem is institutional decoupling, in which firms comply on paper while core practices remain unchanged, with material implications for investor confidence and the region's progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (Lueg & Lueg, 2020;van der Lugt & Mans Kemp, 2020). 

The review pursues four integrated objectives: i. 

To analyze the evidence around governance flaws, reporting gaps and misleading sustainability claims among regional corporations, examining associated drivers and reform options ii. 

To evaluate policy, regulatory, and assurance weaknesses enabling greenwashing behaviors to persist across sub-Saharan jurisdictions amid rhetorical adoption of ESG ideals iii. 

To assess economic, social, and environmental consequences from the failure to effectively incentivize authentic corporate sustainability in the region iv. 

To explore innovations around standards, disclosures, auditing, and monitoring that can enhance accountability to advance progress against Africa's sustainable development priorities 

The review further addresses two questions that frame the analysis: 

v. 

What governance and market conditions most consistently enable greenwashing and social washing in African corporate practice? vi. 

Which regulatory, assurance, and digital interventions show the strongest promise to close the disclosure performance gap and align corporate behaviour with sustainable development priorities? 

This paper is organized as follows: immediately after the introduction, the literature review follows, synthesizing the literature on ESG, followed by background information on the research and methodology. After the analysis and findings of the study, the authors provide discussions and implications. Finally, this paper concludes with key points, recommendations, and future research directions.

Title: Sustainability Reporting and Discretionary Accruals of Multinational Corporations in Sub-Saharan Africa
Snippet: This segment of the paper discusses the study's methodology. Ex-post facto research design was adopted to explore how sustainability reporting can affect the discretionary accruals of earnings management of multinational companies of sub-Saharan Africa countries. This research design assumed that cause-effect relationships exist between the variables of sustainability reporting and discretionary accruals. 

All the quoted multinational entities in sub-Saharan Africa countries of Zaire, Mauritius, Zimbabwe, United Republic of Tanzania, Burundi, Uganda, Kenya, Niger, Botswana, Somalia, Malawi, Ethiopia, Benin, South Africa, Angola, Togo, Cameroon, , Liberia,, Mauritania, Cote d'Ivoire, Guinea-Bissau, Sierra Leone, Zambia, Burkina Faso, Gambia, Central African Republic, Gabon, Chad, Nigeria, Guinea, Congo, Rwanda, Namibia, Ghana, Lesotho, Mozambique, Senegal, Madagascar, and Eritreaas at 31st December 2010 -2019 constituted the study's population. Data about the variables of the research work were derived from the audited financial statement of the sampled listed multinational companies in Sub-Saharan Africa countries. 

The Purposive and judgmental sampling techniques were adopted for the work. These techniques were suitable for picking the listed multinational companies in sub-Saharan Africa countries firms which passed the following three criteria. The corporations picked were listed in stock exchanges whose financial records as well as sustainability disclosures in accordance with the guidelines of Global Reporting Initiatives (GRI) were audited under enabling statutes and readily available for review for the period under review (2010)(2011)(2012)(2013)(2014)(2015)(2016)(2017)(2018)(2019). 

Following the aforementioned benchmarks, fifty (50) multinational firms were selected, five (5) multinational companies were selected each from ten (10) of the sub-Saharan Africa countries whose capital market was relatively developed or developing. The countries are Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Nigeria, Malawi, Kenya, Botswana, Zambia, Ghana, South Africa, and Mauritius 

We adopted content analysis to analyze the contents of the annual financial reports and accounts as well as the sustainability reports of the selected multinational companies. The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the various Stock Exchanges of the selected multinational companies were adopted to access the degree of compliance of the firms to sustainability reporting disclosures.

snippet.text:
Amidst the vast and diverse landscapes of sub-Saharan Africa, the energy sector has emerged as a powerful catalyst driving economic progress and development, energizing industries, homes, and communities alike. However, this relentless growth in energy demand, propelled by a burgeoning population and expanding economies, comes hand in hand with an equally pressing challenge: environmental sustainability. 

In 2021, environmental sustainability took center stage as over 40,000 people, including 120 world leaders, 22,274 party delegates, 14,124 observers, and 3,886 media representatives, gathered in Glasgow, Scotland for the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP26). The event spanned two weeks and captivated global attention, with evidence, solutions, political will to act, and concrete signals of climate change action at the forefront of discussions (UN, 2021). Environmental disclosure has emerged as a crucial instrument at this critical juncture to address climate change and its consequences, offering valuable insights into corporate responsibility and transparency. 

Environmental disclosure can be considered critical for fostering stakeholder engagement and driving the "greening" of corporate financial reports. Tukur, Shehu, Mammadi, and Sulaiman (2019) stated that a firm can carry out corporate social responsibility by involving environmental conservation and sustainability activities. According to Nweze and Nwadialor (2020), environmental disclosure entails disclosing expenses incurred by a company to preserve and enhance its local environment in its annual report. In doing so, firms become more transparent about their investments in environmental protection, particularly when these expenditures are linked to operations that negatively impact the natural world. 

In light of this, Jeroh (2020) highlights the significance of listed firms in sub-Saharan Africa, especially those in the energy industry, reporting their environmental obligations to the public. Failure to do so may hinder transparency, accountability, and the acquisition of legitimacy and recognition from stakeholders. This has prompted numerous studies underlining the need for better environmental performance, disclosure standards, and further recommendations for businesses to adopt eco-friendly practices. Environmental disclosure has emerged as a central discourse in accounting literature because of the mounting pressure to fulfill many environmental obligations across various industries. 

Regrettably, despite the increasing emphasis on environmental sustainability, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the factors influencing environmental disclosure practices among sub-Saharan African energy firms.

According to Lashitew (2021), the rapid diffusion of sustainability rhetoric across African markets has outpaced the development and enforcement of credible governance, creating fertile conditions for environmental, social, and governance malpractices that erode trust and misallocate capital. The persistent gap between disclosure and performance has been documented in South Africa's building sector, cotton certification in multiple African countries, and investment markets in Zimbabwe, where selective reporting and weak assurance enable symbolic rather than substantive change to dominate corporate communication ecosystems (Schoeman & Gunter, 2018;Partzsch et al., 2019;Olatubosun & Nyazenga, 2021). This study argues that the central problem is institutional decoupling, in which firms comply on paper while core practices remain unchanged, with material implications for investor confidence and the region's progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (Lueg & Lueg, 2020;van der Lugt & Mans Kemp, 2020). 

The review pursues four integrated objectives: i. 

To analyze the evidence around governance flaws, reporting gaps and misleading sustainability claims among regional corporations, examining associated drivers and reform options ii. 

To evaluate policy, regulatory, and assurance weaknesses enabling greenwashing behaviors to persist across sub-Saharan jurisdictions amid rhetorical adoption of ESG ideals iii. 

To assess economic, social, and environmental consequences from the failure to effectively incentivize authentic corporate sustainability in the region iv. 

To explore innovations around standards, disclosures, auditing, and monitoring that can enhance accountability to advance progress against Africa's sustainable development priorities 

The review further addresses two questions that frame the analysis: 

v. 

What governance and market conditions most consistently enable greenwashing and social washing in African corporate practice? vi. 

Which regulatory, assurance, and digital interventions show the strongest promise to close the disclosure performance gap and align corporate behaviour with sustainable development priorities? 

This paper is organized as follows: immediately after the introduction, the literature review follows, synthesizing the literature on ESG, followed by background information on the research and methodology. After the analysis and findings of the study, the authors provide discussions and implications. Finally, this paper concludes with key points, recommendations, and future research directions.

This segment of the paper discusses the study's methodology. Ex-post facto research design was adopted to explore how sustainability reporting can affect the discretionary accruals of earnings management of multinational companies of sub-Saharan Africa countries. This research design assumed that cause-effect relationships exist between the variables of sustainability reporting and discretionary accruals. 

All the quoted multinational entities in sub-Saharan Africa countries of Zaire, Mauritius, Zimbabwe, United Republic of Tanzania, Burundi, Uganda, Kenya, Niger, Botswana, Somalia, Malawi, Ethiopia, Benin, South Africa, Angola, Togo, Cameroon, , Liberia,, Mauritania, Cote d'Ivoire, Guinea-Bissau, Sierra Leone, Zambia, Burkina Faso, Gambia, Central African Republic, Gabon, Chad, Nigeria, Guinea, Congo, Rwanda, Namibia, Ghana, Lesotho, Mozambique, Senegal, Madagascar, and Eritreaas at 31st December 2010 -2019 constituted the study's population. Data about the variables of the research work were derived from the audited financial statement of the sampled listed multinational companies in Sub-Saharan Africa countries. 

The Purposive and judgmental sampling techniques were adopted for the work. These techniques were suitable for picking the listed multinational companies in sub-Saharan Africa countries firms which passed the following three criteria. The corporations picked were listed in stock exchanges whose financial records as well as sustainability disclosures in accordance with the guidelines of Global Reporting Initiatives (GRI) were audited under enabling statutes and readily available for review for the period under review (2010)(2011)(2012)(2013)(2014)(2015)(2016)(2017)(2018)(2019). 

Following the aforementioned benchmarks, fifty (50) multinational firms were selected, five (5) multinational companies were selected each from ten (10) of the sub-Saharan Africa countries whose capital market was relatively developed or developing. The countries are Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Nigeria, Malawi, Kenya, Botswana, Zambia, Ghana, South Africa, and Mauritius 

We adopted content analysis to analyze the contents of the annual financial reports and accounts as well as the sustainability reports of the selected multinational companies. The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the various Stock Exchanges of the selected multinational companies were adopted to access the degree of compliance of the firms to sustainability reporting disclosures.

documents.title: Corporate responsibility or corporate illusion? An integrative review analysis of the Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) shortcomings and greenwashing in Sub-Saharan Africa
documents.snippet: This study examines how environmental, social, and governance malpractices manifest as selective disclosure and weak assurance, enabling greenwashing across corporations in sub–Saharan Africa, and delineates governance and policy levers to curb these behaviors. Following integrative review standards, the study screens Scopus and Web of Science outputs and synthesizes 22 peer-reviewed studies published between 2014 and 2024 using a transparent PRISMA-informed pipeline and thematic coding to ensure replicability and analytic depth. The evidence shows that greenwashing is driven by regulatory gaps, voluntary compliance regimes, and narrative heavy self-reporting, while quality of integrated reporting is unevenly translated into real performance, signalling persistent decoupling between disclosure and outcomes; the preponderance of studies identifies governance weaknesses and selective disclosures as recurrent enablers across sectors including certification schemes and the built environment, corroborating the dominance of symbolic over substantive implementation in many African settings. The review argues for stronger ESG legislation, independent third-party auditing, and digital monitoring tools to restore investor confidence, protect public trust, and align corporate behaviour with the Sustainable Development Goals in sub-Saharan Africa

documents.snippet:
Despite a significant cultural and socioeconomic difference, little is understood about the interaction of cultural and social contexts with reporting, beyond the images of extreme poverty repeatedly documented in the media (Waweru 2020). However, there is a paucity of studies on the impact of corporate governance on ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). To the best of our knowledge, the only available studies are Waweru (2020), which analyses the disclosure of business ethics and corporate governance in sub-Saharan Africa, together with Githaiga and Kosgei (2023), that examined the board characteristics and sustainability reporting of selected firms from countries in East Africa. Nonetheless, ESG disclosure in sub-Saharan Africa has gained traction as companies recognise the need to address ESG concerns, with the aim of creating value, building trust and contributing to solving significant challenges (Tilt et al. 2021). 

In terms of companies in sub-Saharan Africa, enhanced ESG disclosure practices are crucial to access funding sources and attract investors (Siueia et al. 2019). Improved corporate disclosure practices, including non-financial disclosures, are becoming increasingly influential as stakeholders demand transparency and accountability (e.g. Amran & Keat Ooi 2014;Maas & Sampers 2020). However, recent studies focusing on sub-Saharan Africa have not yet confirmed this evidence. Notably, Githaiga and Kosgei (2023), examined the correlation between the board characteristics and sustainability reporting of listed firms in East Africa. The findings they obtained underlined that board gender diversity, board financial expertise and board independence are positively and significantly associated with sustainability reporting, whereas board size has a negative and significant effect on sustainability reporting. Similarly, Ofoegbu et al. (2018) examined corporate board characteristics and environmental disclosure quantity based on South Africa (integrated reporting) and Nigeria (traditional reporting). The authors determined a significant positive relationship between board independence and environmental disclosure in Nigeria. The research they conducted focused on individual nations or a specific economic bloc. Given that the sub-Saharan region comprises the largest part of the continent, the understanding derived from these particular studies has substantial implications not only for the entire region of Africa, but also for other emerging economies that share similar developmental characteristics.

attempts.answer:
Summary and framing
Treating “Sub-Saharan Africa” as a single geographic unit risks masking meaningful cross-country heterogeneity because enforcement of IFRS, capital market depth, and legal origins vary widely across the region and each shapes firms’ incentives to disclose and the credibility of financial reporting. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">Even when countries adopt uniform standards like IFRS, differences in legal and political systems, enforcement, and litigation meaningfully affect reporting quality and outcomes, so results from advanced-country settings often do not generalize to Africa</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-1">Within SSA, weak monitoring and uneven enforcement of IFRS compliance are common features, implying that the benefits of international standards may materialize unevenly across jurisdictions</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-2">Research coverage of IFRS and accounting quality in SSA remains sparse and often focuses on compliance and disclosure rather than core reporting quality metrics</cite>.

Why “Sub-Saharan Africa” is too coarse a unit for climate disclosure–reporting quality analyses
1) IFRS adoption and enforcement vary, altering incentives and credibility. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">IFRS quality effects depend on how standards are interpreted, enforced, and litigated; absent a global regulator, effectiveness varies by country, and outcomes do not converge across jurisdictions</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-1">In SSA, lax monitoring and weak enforcement of IFRS compliance are documented, with studies emphasizing that the mere adoption of higher-quality standards does not guarantee improved reporting quality</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-4">Empirical work across African countries shows that macroeconomic and financial market development factors influence IFRS adoption patterns, implying that the level of harmonization does not wipe out domestic institutional differences</cite>. These differences matter because climate risk disclosure is increasingly tied to accounting choices (e.g., asset recognition and impairment) and recognized in IFRS 17/18 contexts; when enforcement and auditing differ, the translation of disclosure into reporting quality will differ. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">Prior cross-country IFRS results often fail to account for variation in legal and political environments and enforcement, reducing external validity for SSA aggregates</cite>.

2) Capital market depth and governance shape disclosure uptake and consequences. <cite id="93dde382-0">Panels of listed firms across SSA show relatively low governance quality indices and nontrivial discretionary accruals, indicating a setting where opportunistic reporting is not rare</cite>. <cite id="93dde382-4">Across seven SSA countries (244 firms, 4,880 observations), political instability is positively associated with earnings management and stronger governance features (audit quality, board independence) are associated with lower accrual-based manipulation</cite>. <cite id="93dde382-1">Studies that pool across multiple SSA exchanges explicitly note that governance systems, investor protections, and regulatory frameworks differ markedly from developed economies, which is crucial for interpreting how climate disclosure affects reporting quality</cite>. Given climate disclosures’ potential to reduce information asymmetry and improve loss recognition and valuation, their impact should differ by market depth and oversight strength.

Snippet: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors have transitioned from niche considerations to central pillars shaping global business strategy, investment decision-making, and regulatory frameworks (Friede, Busch & Bassen, 2015). The establishment of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) and the introduction of IFRS S1 and S2 standards have marked critical milestones, providing a coherent global structure for ESG disclosures with particular emphasis on climate-related risks and sustainability-driven financial reporting (IFRS Foundation, 2023). This global momentum is mirrored in the European Union's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), which enforces doublemateriality disclosures mandating that firms report both financial and non-financial ESG impacts. In parallel, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has advanced climate-related disclosure requirements, and nations such as Singapore, Canada, and the United Kingdom have integrated ESG principles into their regulatory frameworks (Biju, 2025). Collectively, these developments signify a universal movement towards standardised ESG reporting, heightened stakeholder accountability, and ethical governance. 

In Africa, the ESG movement is gaining significant traction. The Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) became the first emerging market exchange to feature a sustainability index in 2004 and has since aligned its Sustainability Disclosure Guidance with IFRS S1 and S2 standards (Matemane et al., 2024). 

South Africa further distinguishes itself through the ratification of the Paris Agreement, the Climate Change Bill, the Carbon Tax Act, and the King IV Report on Corporate Governance, which promotes integrated reporting and ethical leadership (Institute of Directors in Southern Africa, 2016). Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and other African nations are similarly advancing ESG regulatory frameworks, with growing regional collaboration driving the ESG agenda forward (Oncioiu et al., 2020). Mauritius has issued sustainable bond guidelines and listed its first green bond in 2023, while Rwanda has prioritised climate finance through its national green bond strategy. 

Within the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the evolution of ESG practices has moved from philanthropy-centred Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) to strategic sustainability integration. Before the 2000s, corporate responsibility primarily involved charitable initiatives such as constructing schools and clinics.

Summary and framing
Treating “Sub-Saharan Africa” as a single geographic unit risks masking meaningful cross-country heterogeneity because enforcement of IFRS, capital market depth, and legal origins vary widely across the region and each shapes firms’ incentives to disclose and the credibility of financial reporting. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">Even when countries adopt uniform standards like IFRS, differences in legal and political systems, enforcement, and litigation meaningfully affect reporting quality and outcomes, so results from advanced-country settings often do not generalize to Africa</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-1">Within SSA, weak monitoring and uneven enforcement of IFRS compliance are common features, implying that the benefits of international standards may materialize unevenly across jurisdictions</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-2">Research coverage of IFRS and accounting quality in SSA remains sparse and often focuses on compliance and disclosure rather than core reporting quality metrics</cite>.

Why “Sub-Saharan Africa” is too coarse a unit for climate disclosure–reporting quality analyses
1) IFRS adoption and enforcement vary, altering incentives and credibility. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">IFRS quality effects depend on how standards are interpreted, enforced, and litigated; absent a global regulator, effectiveness varies by country, and outcomes do not converge across jurisdictions</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-1">In SSA, lax monitoring and weak enforcement of IFRS compliance are documented, with studies emphasizing that the mere adoption of higher-quality standards does not guarantee improved reporting quality</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-4">Empirical work across African countries shows that macroeconomic and financial market development factors influence IFRS adoption patterns, implying that the level of harmonization does not wipe out domestic institutional differences</cite>. These differences matter because climate risk disclosure is increasingly tied to accounting choices (e.g., asset recognition and impairment) and recognized in IFRS 17/18 contexts; when enforcement and auditing differ, the translation of disclosure into reporting quality will differ. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">Prior cross-country IFRS results often fail to account for variation in legal and political environments and enforcement, reducing external validity for SSA aggregates</cite>.

2) Capital market depth and governance shape disclosure uptake and consequences. <cite id="93dde382-0">Panels of listed firms across SSA show relatively low governance quality indices and nontrivial discretionary accruals, indicating a setting where opportunistic reporting is not rare</cite>. <cite id="93dde382-4">Across seven SSA countries (244 firms, 4,880 observations), political instability is positively associated with earnings management and stronger governance features (audit quality, board independence) are associated with lower accrual-based manipulation</cite>. <cite id="93dde382-1">Studies that pool across multiple SSA exchanges explicitly note that governance systems, investor protections, and regulatory frameworks differ markedly from developed economies, which is crucial for interpreting how climate disclosure affects reporting quality</cite>. Given climate disclosures’ potential to reduce information asymmetry and improve loss recognition and valuation, their impact should differ by market depth and oversight strength.

3) Legal origin differences condition disclosure orientation and quality. <cite id="2ad38b7a-2">Common-law systems tend to emphasize judicial interpretation and investor-oriented financial reporting, while civil-law systems rely on codified statutes and tax-oriented reporting; these differences lead to different disclosure emphases and mixed findings on the quality and value relevance of financial statements across legal regimes</cite>. <cite id="2ad38b7a-1">Empirical work links legal origin to disclosure levels, with common-law countries often requiring and using more disclosure to mitigate agency problems, whereas civil-law countries’ insider ownership and legislative codification reduce disclosure demands</cite>. Within SSA, countries like South Africa (legal origin common law) and Morocco (civil law) exhibit different reporting frameworks and governance pressures, implying that the same climate disclosure practices can have heterogeneous effects on reporting quality. <cite id="2ad38b7a-0">Even within countries of the same legal system, differences in reporting mandates (e.g., South Africa’s integrated reporting vs. Nigeria’s traditional reporting) produce different disclosure environments, underscoring that legal origin is necessary but not sufficient to pin down effects</cite>. <cite id="2ad38b7a-4">Comparative legal system research further cautions that the civil/common-law classification can oversimplify and that enforcement and institutional specifics matter</cite>.

Climate risk disclosure’s uneven institutional context in SSA
Climate/ESG disclosure is evolving unevenly across SSA, with South Africa further along and others lagging, which complicates a one-size analysis. <cite id="ce43e34b-2">The JSE was the first emerging market to launch a sustainability index and has aligned its sustainability disclosure guidance with IFRS S1/S2, and South Africa has enacted climate-related laws (Paris Agreement, Climate Change Bill, Carbon Tax Act) and adopted King IV’s integrated reporting</cite>. <cite id="ce43e34b-2">Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and other countries are advancing ESG frameworks, but alignment is still developing</cite>. <cite id="ce43e34b-4">A review of ESG shortcomings and greenwashing in SSA finds that while sustainability governance infrastructure exists (e.g., King Code, JSE ESG rules, GRI/SDG references), integrity issues and enforcement gaps still permit misconduct, pointing to persistent implementation challenges</cite>. <cite id="ce43e34b-3">Broader governance work highlights underdeveloped regulatory frameworks, inconsistent enforcement, market informality, and political instability as structural obstacles that hinder robust disclosure practices</cite>. In this patchwork, climate risk disclosure’s effect on reporting quality (e.g., lower discretionary accruals, improved impairment timeliness, greater value relevance) is unlikely to be uniform across SSA unless models explicitly allow heterogeneity.

Empirical designs using SSA samples that nonetheless aggregate
Some SSA studies do analyze the region as a pool yet explicitly recognize heterogeneity across countries and emphasize cross-country comparability challenges. <cite id="93dde382-1">For example, a panel spanning nine SSA exchanges constructs a balanced sample across 10 countries to study accrual earnings management, noting that governance and regulatory frameworks differ from developed economies and cautioning about external validity</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-2">Studies on IFRS and transparency in SSA examine adoption levels across 31 SSA countries and test institutional quality as a mediator, acknowledging that prior research underemphasized comparability effects and institutional variation</cite>. These designs provide templates for SSA-wide analyses that should incorporate interaction terms for IFRS enforcement, legal origin, and market depth to avoid biased inference.

Methodological guidance: when regional aggregation is unavoidable
If you proceed with a Sub-Saharan Africa aggregate, adopt defensibility measures:
- Use country and exchange fixed effects and IFRS/reporting regime indicators to absorb omitted-variable bias from uneven enforcement and standards alignment. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">Because reporting quality varies with enforcement and litigation environments, fixed effects that capture national institutional regimes can mitigate aggregation bias</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-1">Dummy variables for IFRS adoption/enforcement intensity and auditor oversight levels can interact with climate disclosure measures to test whether disclosure translates into higher reporting quality only where enforcement is stronger</cite>.
- Interact climate disclosure metrics with instruments of market depth and governance (e.g., analyst coverage, board independence, audit quality indices) to test heterogeneous effects. <cite id="93dde382-4">Evidence that audit quality and board independence reduce earnings management suggests that the marginal benefit of climate disclosure on reporting quality may be larger in strong-institution subgroups</cite>.
- Allow heterogeneous slopes by legal origin and common vs. civil law, and by presence of integrated reporting mandates. <cite id="2ad38b7a-2">Legal systems differ in investor orientation and regulatory design, so climate disclosure–reporting quality effects may differ by origin</cite>. <cite id="2ad38b7a-0">Within-law heterogeneity (e.g., integrated reporting in South Africa vs. traditional reporting in Nigeria) implies that legal origin main effects should be tested with interaction terms for local reporting rules</cite>.
- Diagnose heterogeneity via interaction terms and heteroskedasticity-robust F-tests; use Chow tests or cluster-robust inference to validate stable effects before treating SSA as a unit. <cite id="2ad38b7a-4">Scholars caution that the civil/common-law binary can be misleading; robustness to alternative legal-classification cuts and within-country variation strengthens causal interpretation</cite>.
- Report sub-sample results for countries with stronger vs. weaker enforcement and different legal origins (e.g., South Africa and Mauritius as stronger; Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya as mixed; others as weaker), and for SSE markets with varying market depth. <cite id="ce43e34b-2">South Africa’s more advanced legal and regulatory infrastructure provides a natural “treatment” subgroup for testing whether climate disclosures improve reporting quality more than in peers</cite>. <cite id="ce43e34b-4">Document enforcement gaps and greenwashing risks when interpreting effects</cite>.

Practical implications for your question
- Is SSA a valid geographic unit? If your hypothesis is that climate risk disclosure improves financial reporting quality “across Sub-Saharan Africa,” the short answer is no unless you interact for enforcement, legal origin, and market depth. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">IFRS adoption alone does not yield uniform quality; legal, political, and enforcement features continue to shape outcomes</cite>. <cite id="3433fd1a-1">Weak monitoring and uneven enforcement in many SSA settings imply that the same disclosure requirements can have little effect where governance is weak</cite>. <cite id="2ad38b7a-2">Legal origin differences alter the information environment and value relevance of financial statements</cite>. <cite id="93dde382-4">Political instability elevates earnings management and governance quality moderates effects</cite>. Given these drivers, a single-region effect is unlikely without interactions.
- If you must aggregate, do so defensively. <cite id="93dde382-1">Include country- and exchange-level fixed effects, IFRS enforcement indicators, and legal origin interactions</cite>. <cite id="ce43e34b-2">Account for JSE-led integrated reporting alignment vs. other exchanges’ earlier/limited ESG adoption</cite>. <cite id="ce43e34b-4">Add controls/mitigants for greenwashing risks and assurance coverage</cite>. If interactions are significant and heterogeneous, treat SSA as an umbrella with subgroups and interpret effects conditionally.
- For climate disclosure’s pathway to reporting quality, consider channels beyond textual disclosure. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">IFRS adoption affects loss recognition and impairment accounting; where enforcement and litigation are stronger, these accounting changes are more credible</cite>. <cite id="93dde382-0">In SSA settings with notable discretionary accruals, climate disclosure may reduce opportunistic accruals more where audit quality and board independence are higher</cite>. <cite id="ce43e34b-2">Integrated reporting and IFRS S1/S2 alignment in South Africa tie climate risks to numbers (e.g., asset impairment, reserves), offering a concrete route from disclosure to reporting quality that may not be present where frameworks are less developed</cite>.

Design blueprint you can use
- Sample and scope: Use panel of listed firms across SSA with clean financials and audit data; include nonfinancials with appropriate adjustments, and exclude banks if your accrual-based quality metric is sensitive to specialized accounting.
- Treatments and outcomes: Climate disclosure score (text-based ESG intensity, IFRS S1/S2 adoption, integrated reporting adoption), and reporting quality proxies (discretionary accruals, loss recognition timeliness, value relevance, audit adjustments).
- Covariates and instruments: IFRS adoption/enforcement indicators; legal origin dummies and interactions with reporting mandates (integrated vs. traditional); market depth (analyst following, SSE turnover), governance (board independence, audit quality ratings), political risk (WGI).
- Models: Two-way fixed effects (country/exchange, time) with interaction terms for climate disclosure × enforcement, disclosure × legal origin, and climate disclosure × governance; cluster standard errors at firm or country level; heterogeneity tests and placebo shocks; robustness to alternative disclosure and quality measures.
- Interpretation: Report SSA-wide point estimates but emphasize subgroup differences; if effects differ significantly by enforcement/legal origin, conclude that SSA is not a valid “heterogeneous unit” for the climate–reporting quality relationship and recommend subgroup analyses or interaction models.

Bottom line
Given strong cross-country variation in IFRS enforcement, legal origins, governance quality, political risk, and uneven development of climate/ESG frameworks, “Sub-Saharan Africa” is generally not a valid geographic unit for a uniform analysis of how climate risk disclosure affects financial reporting quality. A defensible approach is to analyze SSA-wide but with explicit interactions for IFRS enforcement, legal origin, and capital market/governance conditions, and to interpret effects conditionally across subgroups; alternatively, stratify samples by country/reporting regime to identify where climate disclosure causally improves reporting quality. <cite id="3433fd1a-0">IFRS adoption does not eliminate institutional heterogeneity in reporting quality</cite> <cite id="3433fd1a-1">and SSA exhibits uneven enforcement and monitoring</cite> <cite id="2ad38b7a-2">with legal-origin-driven differences in disclosure orientation and quality</cite> <cite id="93dde382-4">and political risk materially elevates earnings management</cite> <cite id="ce43e34b-2">while ESG/climate disclosure regimes develop unevenly across exchanges</cite> <cite id="ce43e34b-4">and greenwashing risks remain where implementation and enforcement are weak</cite>. </answer>

Title: The Effects of International Financial Reporting Standards on Reporting Quality of Financial Institutions in Ghana
Snippet: Palea (2013) posits that country"s legal and political systems as well as financial reporting incentives tend to shape the quality of accounting of that country.Indeed, the application of IAS reflects combined effects of features of the financial reporting system, including standards, their interpretation, enforcement, and litigation (Barth, Landsman, & Lang, 2008b).

Title: IFRS adoption and foreign direct investment in Sub-Saharan African countries: Does the levels of Adoption Matter?
Snippet: Bushman and Smith (2001) suggested three channels through which financial accounting information might influence economic performance: 1) Improved project identification by managers and investors; 2) Discipline in project selection and expropriation by managers; and 3) Lessening of investor information asymmetries. Moreover, in the long term, the harmonization of the accounting standards would improve trust and familiarity, improving investor confidence, enhancing market liquidity and reducing the cost of capital and hence increasing flows of foreign investment between countries (Márquez-Ramos, 2008). Countries where the transparency of financial reports is poor, relative to the transparency provided under IFRS, have the greatest potential for increasing transparency through IFRS adoption. In general, countries with developing economies have weaker domestic financial reporting regulations, with less transparency in their financial reports, than countries with developed economies (Ding et al., 2007).

It therefore, becomes pretty crucial that more research on the effect of IFRS adoption on the continent of African be undertaken in order to get a better picture of the situation in the region considering the fact that majority of prior studies focused mainly on European and other advanced countries with very few directed at Africa, more especially, the sub-Saharan Africa (Ames, 2013;Samaha & Khlif, 2016) to better inform strategic policy direction.

Title: Corporate board characteristics and environmental disclosure quantity: Evidence from South Africa (integrated reporting) and Nigeria (traditional reporting)
Snippet: We provided evidence on corporate board characteristics influence on environmental disclosure quantity of quoted firms in South Africa and Nigeria. Furthermore, we chose South Africa and Nigeria (two common law countries), unlike Khlif et al. (2015) that investigated the relationship between corporate performance and social and environmental disclosure of South Africa (common law country) and Morocco (civil law country). Though these two African leading economies have the same legal system, a reasonable gap exists between the two nations in their corporate reporting framework for quoted firms. South African quoted companies are mandated to submit an integrated annual report as approved by the King III report (Rensburg & Botha, 2014;Zhou, Simnett, & Green, 2017). While in Nigeria, the traditional corporate annual reporting is still a vital medium of relating to the stakeholders, which Otu Umoren, John Udo, and Sunday George (2015) found to be lacking relevant information concerning the natural capital and other non-financial issues. The empirical evidence on the determinants of disclosure decisions is largely inconclusive (Beyer, Cohen, Lys, & Walther, 2010;Gray, Javad, Power, & Sinclair, 2001;Ott, Schiemann, & Günther, 2017). 

Our study contributes to accounting literature on the determinants of corporate environmental disclosure (Khlif et al., 2015). For the first time, we provide evidence between two countries of the same legal system but have different reporting mechanisms. 

The rest of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 the theoretical framework, literature review, and hypotheses development. Section 3 discusses the research methodology, and Section 4 explains the results and discussion. Finally, Section 5 conclusions and limitations as well as directions for future studies.

Title: Determinants of Islamic Social Reporting in Indonesia and Malaysia
Snippet: Legal origin has been proven to affect the level of disclosure in a country [10,11]. La Porta et al. [12] and Ball et al. [13] have examined the legal origin factors that comprise common and civil laws. Both legal origins (common and civil laws) have different agency problems. In common law countries, companies have a higher number of transactions with other parties (investors) and thus require more disclosure [13]. In civil law countries, the majority of companies is owned by insiders who get direct information from management; hence, the disclosure requirement is less [10]. Roe (1994) in Ball [13] states that disclosure standards in common law countries are higher thereby reducing agency problems. 

H5: Legal origins affect the level of ISR disclosure.

Title: Examining the value relevance of financial statements in European countries: the importance of legal origins on cross listing decisions
Snippet: the legal system is typically divided into two categories: common law and civil law. common law countries prioritize the judiciary's role in interpreting and enforcing the law, whereas civil law countries emphasize codified laws and the legislature's role in shaping legal frameworks. this distinction leads to differing emphases on financial reporting practices. common law countries place greater importance on the information provided by financial statements, while civil law countries focus more on regulatory compliance. in civil law countries, the government establishes accounting principles through legislation, resulting in a strong tax orientation in financial reporting. credit institutions are the primary source of external finance for the private sector, leading to bank-based financial systems. in contrast, professional regulatory bodies set accounting principles in common law countries, and external capital for business entities comes primarily from the capital market. therefore, financial reporting in common law countries has a strong investor orientation, resulting in market-based financial systems (Filip et al., 2015;hevas et al., 2009;la Porta et al., 1998;2008). empirical research has investigated how the quality and relevance of financial statements differ across common law and civil law countries. While several studies have examined the relationship between the quality of financial statements, relevance, and legal systems, their findings are contradicting. For instance, Filip et al. (2015), finds that the civil law framework in France incentivizes companies to disclose superior quality financial information. this is due to the amplified exposure to liability, that auditors and corporate directors face under the aforementioned legal regime. in contrast, Kang (2003) found that the legal regime has a marginal impact on the value-relevance of accounting information, suggesting that common law may be associated with higher accounting relevance. additionally, Wulandari (2005) found that the quality, acceptability, and enforceability of accounting standards are important for the usefulness of accounting earnings in a country, and that the accounting institutional environment has a stronger positive association with the value relevance of earnings than the legal environment has. Finally, according to lindahl and schadéwitz ( 2013), the belief that common law offers a more stable basis for ensuring accounting transparency than civil law is being questioned. they argue that the application of the civil/ common classification in accounting research lacks support.

Title: The Threshold Effects of National Governance Quality on the Earnings Management – Performance Nexus: Evidence From Dynamic Panel Threshold Regression
Snippet: Descriptive Statistics. Tables 2 and 3 summarize the descriptive statistics and correlation diagnostics for the variables in the study. The mean Return on Assets (ROA) stands at 8.03%, suggesting comparable returns earned by financiers to companies in Sub-Saharan Africa during the sample period to those reported in other countries (Elkalla, 2017). The Corporate Governance Quality (CGQ) and National Governance Quality (NGQ) indices exhibit means of 20.209 and 0.0267, respectively, on a scale ranging from 21.294 to + 2.334. These aggregate governance indices for sampled companies in Sub-Saharan Africa indicate low levels, reflecting minimal progress in developing national and corporate governance institutions within the African subregion. 

The average amount of discretionary accruals, or the proportion of managed earnings for sampled companies, was approximately 0.020, comparable to figures reported in other emerging economies (Tang & Chang, 2015;Zimon et al., 2021), and suggest the prevalence of earnings management practices among firms in Sub-Saharan Africa. The average firm size, expressed logarithmically, was 5.29, with a standard deviation of 0.72, while the average leverage was 3.81, with a standard deviation of 0.69. These metrics, presented in logarithmic form so as to normalize their histogram distributions for Note. This table reports descriptive statistics based on a balanced sample with 676 observations. The variables are as defined in Table 1. For interpretation purposes, the descriptive statistics are calculated on the basis of levels with the exception of IFRS Adoption which was computed from a dummy scale, CGQ and NGQ which were calculated as indices from normalized rotated principal component analysis, and Firm Size, Age and Leverage which were calculated on the basis of logarithmic form to normalize their histogram distributions for a meaningful statistical analysis. The ROA, being the dependent variable in our model, was not transformed but allowed to retain its original form for 1) ease of interpretations, 2) because its histogram distribution appears normal. With a mean market-to-book ratio of 3.72 and a standard deviation of 5.62, the sampled firms displayed moderately strong growth opportunities with occasional erratic surges in growth.

Title: Re-examining the accrual earnings management–firm performance nexus: new insights from panel threshold regression and the panopticon metaphor
Snippet: The study draws its sample from non-financial firms listed on nine stock exchanges in Sub-Saharan Africa. Data were sourced from the Africanfinancials and Machameratios databases, yielding an initial sample of 107 firms based on audited annual reports spanning 2007-2019. Due to missing observations, a balanced panel of 52 firms was retained for the final analysis. 

The study period (2007-2019) is appropriate as it captures the post-global financial crisis environment, a period during which firms increasingly relied on earnings management to signal stability. This provides a suitable context for examining the study's hypotheses. Additionally, post-2019 audited reports for many Sub-Saharan African firms were largely unavailable at the time of data collection (completed in December 2022), mainly due to reporting lags and COVID-19-related disruptions. The dataset therefore represents the most complete and consistent cross-country information available. The sample selection procedure is presented in Table 1. 

Financial firms, including banks, are excluded due to their distinct accounting structures, which complicate the estimation of discretionary accruals (see also, [31,100]). While this limits generalizability, the study is intentionally designed to provide context-specific insights into earnings management behaviour within African institutional settings, where governance systems, investor protections, and regulatory frameworks differ markedly from those in developed economies. The variables and their measurements are summarized in Table 2.

Title: Financial reporting quality and the performance of firms in Sub-Sahara Africa: The mediating role of firms’ characteristics
Snippet: Recent studies by Asyik, Agustia, and Muchlis (2023); Ogbonnaya and Amauwa (2019); Rathnayake, Rajapakse, and Lasantha (2021);and Sani, Nasir, Ahmad, and Bakare (2023)suggest that high-quality financial accounting information has the tendency to influence firms' performance. 

Regardless of the fact that there are robust empirical studies on financial reporting quality in both developed and developing countries, these studies were mainly focused on assessing the relationship between financial reporting quality, audit quality, corporate governance, firm value, and performance, amongst others. 

Arguably, there are limited numbers of empirical studies that have assessed whether firms' characteristics (particularly firm size) mediate the relationship between financial reporting quality (FIRQ) and the performance of firms in sub-Saharan Africa. Consequently, there is literature and geographical gaps as to whether firm size mediates the relationship between FIRQ and the performance of firms in sub -Saharan Africa; the gaps that this study sought to satisfy. The study focused mainly on measuring financial performance via return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE), firms' characteristics using the natural logarithm of total assets (size), and financial reporting quality using discretionary cash flows from operating activities less net profit. Furthermore, after determining the mediating role of firms' characteristics in the relationship between financial reporting quality and performance, it would enable us to identify the effect when firms generate quality financial accounting information and what will result from having poor quality financial accounting information for decisionmakers, holding the size of the firm constant. Arising from the above, it is pertinent to raise the following question: to what extent do firms' characteristics mediate the relationship between financial reporting quality and the performance of firms in sub-Saharan Africa? The remaining part of this paper is divided into: Review of Related Literature; Methodology; Results and Discussions; Conclusion and Recommendations.

Title: Influence of Corporate Governance on Financial Performance of Listed Firms in Germany
Snippet: This suggests that enhanced transparency and reporting standards contribute to better financial outcomes, reflecting a growing emphasis on corporate governance and accountability in the region. However, Sub-Saharan economies continue to experience economic instability, currency fluctuations, and limited access to capital markets, which hinder financial performance (Mali & Lim, 2023). Despite these constraints, businesses that implement sound financial management and technological innovations tend to achieve higher returns (Derun & Kasyanov, 2021). 

Standard Bank Group, South Africa's largest bank, reported an ROE of 18.2% in 2023, reflecting steady growth driven by digital banking expansion and risk management improvements (Business Day, 2024). In contrast, Kenya's Equity Group Holdings recorded a decline in its Tobin's Q from 1.6 in 2022 to 1.3 in 2023, attributed to macroeconomic instability and rising interest rates (CBK, 2024). These trends indicate that while some Sub-Saharan African firms are strengthening their financial performance, economic volatility remains a critical challenge (Nzimande & Padia, 2020). Strengthening governance, expanding financial inclusion, and leveraging technology are key strategies for improving financial performance in the region (Derun & Kasyanov, 2021). 

In Nigeria, studies show that firms with higher Return on Assets (ROA) and Tobin's Q tend to attract more investment and achieve better financial outcomes (Oluwagbemiga, 2023). Additionally, in South Africa, there is evidence of a strong relationship between integrated reporting and improved financial performance, with companies that adopt transparent financial reporting achieving higher EPS (Nzimande & Padia, 2020). These findings suggest that enhancing corporate governance practices is essential for driving sustainable financial growth in the region. 

Corporate governance encompasses mechanisms such as board size, CEO duality, ownership structure, and board diversity, which are pivotal in shaping a firm's strategic direction and accountability. Board size refers to the total number of directors on a company's board; an optimal size can enhance decision-making and oversight, positively influencing financial metrics like Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE) (Yermack, 1996).

Title: Impact of Political Instability on Financial Reporting Quality in Sub-Saharan African Countries
Snippet: Purpose: This study investigates how political instability influences the quality of financial reporting in Sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on discretionary accruals as a measure of earnings management. It aims to assess how fragile political systems contribute to reduced financial transparency and increased manipulation in corporate reporting within emerging market contexts.Methodology: Using a balanced panel of 244 listed firms from seven Sub-Saharan African countries between 2004 and 2023 (4,880 firm-year observations), the study employs pooled OLS, fixed effects, and system GMM estimators. Political risk data are sourced from the Worldwide Governance Indicators, while firm-level financials are extracted from annual reports. Diagnostic tests, including the Hausman test and cross-sectional dependence checks, ensure robust model selection and validity.Findings: The analysis reveals a positive and significant relationship between political instability and discretionary accruals, suggesting greater earnings manipulation in politically unstable environments. Conversely, audit quality and board independence are associated with reduced accrual-based earnings management, supporting agency and institutional theory perspectives on governance and transparency.Practical Implications: The findings emphasize the need for stronger institutional frameworks, independent audit oversight, and effective board governance in politically volatile economies. These measures can help reduce opportunistic reporting and enhance investor confidence in financial disclosures.Originality: This study synthesizes six theoretical perspectives to explain how political risk affects corporate reporting. It offers rare empirical insights from Sub-Saharan Africa and applies rigorous econometric techniques to advance the literature on governance and financial reporting.

Regardless of the fact that there are robust empirical studies on financial reporting quality in both developed and developing countries, these studies were mainly focused on assessing the relationship between financial reporting quality, audit quality, corporate governance, firm value, and performance, amongst others. 

Arguably, there are limited numbers of empirical studies that have assessed whether firms' characteristics (particularly firm size) mediate the relationship between financial reporting quality (FIRQ) and the performance of firms in sub-Saharan Africa. Consequently, there is literature and geographical gaps as to whether firm size mediates the relationship between FIRQ and the performance of firms in sub -Saharan Africa; the gaps that this study sought to satisfy. The study focused mainly on measuring financial performance via return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE), firms' characteristics using the natural logarithm of total assets (size), and financial reporting quality using discretionary cash flows from operating activities less net profit. Furthermore, after determining the mediating role of firms' characteristics in the relationship between financial reporting quality and performance, it would enable us to identify the effect when firms generate quality financial accounting information and what will result from having poor quality financial accounting information for decisionmakers, holding the size of the firm constant. Arising from the above, it is pertinent to raise the following question: to what extent do firms' characteristics mediate the relationship between financial reporting quality and the performance of firms in sub-Saharan Africa? However, Sub-Saharan economies continue to experience economic instability, currency fluctuations, and limited access to capital markets, which hinder financial performance (Mali & Lim, 2023). Despite these constraints, businesses that implement sound financial management and technological innovations tend to achieve higher returns (Derun & Kasyanov, 2021). 

Standard Bank Group, South Africa's largest bank, reported an ROE of 18.2% in 2023, reflecting steady growth driven by digital banking expansion and risk management improvements (Business Day, 2024). In contrast, Kenya's Equity Group Holdings recorded a decline in its Tobin's Q from 1.6 in 2022 to 1.3 in 2023, attributed to macroeconomic instability and rising interest rates (CBK, 2024). These trends indicate that while some Sub-Saharan African firms are strengthening their financial performance, economic volatility remains a critical challenge (Nzimande & Padia, 2020). Strengthening governance, expanding financial inclusion, and leveraging technology are key strategies for improving financial performance in the region (Derun & Kasyanov, 2021). 

In Nigeria, studies show that firms with higher Return on Assets (ROA) and Tobin's Q tend to attract more investment and achieve better financial outcomes (Oluwagbemiga, 2023). Additionally, in South Africa, there is evidence of a strong relationship between integrated reporting and improved financial performance, with companies that adopt transparent financial reporting achieving higher EPS (Nzimande & Padia, 2020). These findings suggest that enhancing corporate governance practices is essential for driving sustainable financial growth in the region. 

Corporate governance encompasses mechanisms such as board size, CEO duality, ownership structure, and board diversity, which are pivotal in shaping a firm's strategic direction and accountability. snippet.text: Purpose: This study investigates how political instability influences the quality of financial reporting in Sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on discretionary accruals as a measure of earnings management. It aims to assess how fragile political systems contribute to reduced financial transparency and increased manipulation in corporate reporting within emerging market contexts.Methodology: Using a balanced panel of 244 listed firms from seven Sub-Saharan African countries between 2004 and 2023 (4,880 firm-year observations), the study employs pooled OLS, fixed effects, and system GMM estimators. Political risk data are sourced from the Worldwide Governance Indicators, while firm-level financials are extracted from annual reports. Diagnostic tests, including the Hausman test and cross-sectional dependence checks, ensure robust model selection and validity.Findings: The analysis reveals a positive and significant relationship between political instability and discretionary accruals, suggesting greater earnings manipulation in politically unstable environments. Conversely, audit quality and board independence are associated with reduced accrual-based earnings management, supporting agency and institutional theory perspectives on governance and transparency.Practical Implications: The findings emphasize the need for stronger institutional frameworks, independent audit oversight, and effective board governance in politically volatile economies. These measures can help reduce opportunistic reporting and enhance investor confidence in financial disclosures.Originality: This study synthesizes six theoretical perspectives to explain how political risk affects corporate reporting. It offers rare empirical insights from Sub-Saharan Africa and applies rigorous econometric techniques to advance the literature on governance and financial reporting.

The study draws its sample from non-financial firms listed on nine stock exchanges in Sub-Saharan Africa. Data were sourced from the Africanfinancials and Machameratios databases, yielding an initial sample of 107 firms based on audited annual reports spanning 2007-2019. Due to missing observations, a balanced panel of 52 firms was retained for the final analysis. 

The study period (2007-2019) is appropriate as it captures the post-global financial crisis environment, a period during which firms increasingly relied on earnings management to signal stability. This provides a suitable context for examining the study's hypotheses. Additionally, post-2019 audited reports for many Sub-Saharan African firms were largely unavailable at the time of data collection (completed in December 2022), mainly due to reporting lags and COVID-19-related disruptions. The dataset therefore represents the most complete and consistent cross-country information available. The sample selection procedure is presented in Table 1. 

Financial firms, including banks, are excluded due to their distinct accounting structures, which complicate the estimation of discretionary accruals (see also, [31,100]). While this limits generalizability, the study is intentionally designed to provide context-specific insights into earnings management behaviour within African institutional settings, where governance systems, investor protections, and regulatory frameworks differ markedly from those in developed economies. The variables and their measurements are summarized in Table 2.

Title: ESG Disclosure Ratings and Corporate Financial Performance: A Comparative Analysis of SADC-Listed Firms (2018–2024)
Snippet: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors have transitioned from niche considerations to central pillars shaping global business strategy, investment decision-making, and regulatory frameworks (Friede, Busch & Bassen, 2015). The establishment of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) and the introduction of IFRS S1 and S2 standards have marked critical milestones, providing a coherent global structure for ESG disclosures with particular emphasis on climate-related risks and sustainability-driven financial reporting (IFRS Foundation, 2023). This global momentum is mirrored in the European Union's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), which enforces doublemateriality disclosures mandating that firms report both financial and non-financial ESG impacts. In parallel, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has advanced climate-related disclosure requirements, and nations such as Singapore, Canada, and the United Kingdom have integrated ESG principles into their regulatory frameworks (Biju, 2025). Collectively, these developments signify a universal movement towards standardised ESG reporting, heightened stakeholder accountability, and ethical governance. 

In Africa, the ESG movement is gaining significant traction. The Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) became the first emerging market exchange to feature a sustainability index in 2004 and has since aligned its Sustainability Disclosure Guidance with IFRS S1 and S2 standards (Matemane et al., 2024). 

South Africa further distinguishes itself through the ratification of the Paris Agreement, the Climate Change Bill, the Carbon Tax Act, and the King IV Report on Corporate Governance, which promotes integrated reporting and ethical leadership (Institute of Directors in Southern Africa, 2016). Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and other African nations are similarly advancing ESG regulatory frameworks, with growing regional collaboration driving the ESG agenda forward (Oncioiu et al., 2020). Mauritius has issued sustainable bond guidelines and listed its first green bond in 2023, while Rwanda has prioritised climate finance through its national green bond strategy. 

Within the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the evolution of ESG practices has moved from philanthropy-centred Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) to strategic sustainability integration. Before the 2000s, corporate responsibility primarily involved charitable initiatives such as constructing schools and clinics.

Title: Exploring the impact of board experience diversity on voluntary disclosure: The moderating role of firm size
Snippet: Wachira and Mathuva (2022) indicate that some unique challenges in the sub-Saharan African region include underdeveloped regulatory frameworks, which lead to inconsistent enforcement of governance standards. Moreover, market dynamics, such as high levels of informality and limited access to capital markets, further complicate the adoption of best governance practices (Waweru, 2020). Additionally, socio-economic factors like political instability, corruption, and varying levels of economic development influence corporate governance effectiveness (Almashhadani, 2021;Arslan & Alqatan, 2020;Naciti et al., 2022). Despite these challenges, there are substantial opportunities for firms that adopt strong governance practices. According to Appiah-Kubi et al. (2020) and Areneke et al. (2022), enhanced corporate governance practices can attract foreign investment, improve operational efficiencies, and build trust with stakeholders, ultimately contributing to economic growth and stability. Moreover, Al-Ahdal et al. (2020) add that robust corporate governance practices strongly influence business performance. This is because, it enhances transparency, accountability, and strategic decision-making. Therefore, by promoting ethical behaviour and sound management, firms in sub-Saharan Africa can enhance their competitiveness and sustainability, contributing to broader economic development and stability. Furthermore, in sub-Saharan Africa, where corporate governance practices are still evolving, voluntary disclosure plays an important role in bridging information gaps and enhancing corporate reputation. Voluntary disclosure according to Zamil et al. (2023) refers to the practice of providing additional information beyond what is legally required, distinguishing it from mandatory disclosure, which is governed by regulatory obligations. Voluntary disclosure includes sharing details about corporate strategies, risk management practices, social responsibility initiatives, and other aspects that offer deeper insights into a firm's operations and governance (Boateng et al., 2022;Charumathi & Ramesh, 2020;Pizzi et al., 2022). Monteiro et al. (2023) further add that the importance of voluntary disclosure lies in its ability to build transparency and accountability within firms, fostering trust and confidence among investors, stakeholders, and the public.

Title: Corporate responsibility or corporate illusion? An integrative review analysis of the Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) shortcomings and greenwashing in Sub-Saharan Africa
Snippet: Mandatory sustainability reporting, integrated reporting codes, responsible investment standards, and industry-specific guidelines and certification are found in Sub-Saharan Africa (Lashitew, 2021;Githaiga, 2024). The analysis shows that South Africa has the most advanced sustainability governance infrastructure on the continent. The King Code corporate governance principles, Johannesburg Stock Exchange ESG disclosure listings rules, social and environmental impact assessment laws, and integrated reporting expectations comprise this infrastructure (Donkor et al., 2021;Agnese, 2024). The young but growing ESG regulatory environments of Nigeria, Kenya, Mauritius, and Ghana often reference international standards like the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), and ISO management systems. Other jurisdictions prefer industry self-regulation through multistakeholder sustainability initiatives like forestry stewardship certification, sustainable textiles partnerships, conflict-free mining, and fair-trade agriculture (Al-Hiyari et 2022; Matemane, 2024). These assurance systems enhance transparency and formalize ESG performance criteria, but integrity issues can still enable corporate misconduct (van Niekerk & Conradie, 2020). Thus, despite good sustainability governance underpinnings, scholarly research shows implementation and enforcement gaps that permit greenwashing (Olatubosun & Nyazenga, 2021;van Niekerk & Conradie, 2020).

Other jurisdictions prefer industry self-regulation through multistakeholder sustainability initiatives like forestry stewardship certification, sustainable textiles partnerships, conflict-free mining, and fair-trade agriculture (Al-Hiyari et 2022; Matemane, 2024). These assurance systems enhance transparency and formalize ESG performance criteria, but integrity issues can still enable corporate misconduct (van Niekerk & Conradie, 2020).
